events.text: The registry office where you copy grain reports has one good inkstone, and it belongs to Senior Clerk Hu, who has worked here twenty-two years without a promotion. Today Hu lends it to you, watches you use it, and says: "You write too well for this room."

choices.text: Thank Hu, and copy the next report even more beautifully

effects.log: The Vice Minister reads your report and asks who wrote it. Hu tells him, with a strange smile.

choices.text: Ask Hu why a hand like that never left this room

effects.log: "I wrote one honest report about a granary," Hu says, "in my second year." That is all, for now.

choices.text: Return the inkstone and buy your own (20 taels)

effects.log: Your own inkstone is not as good. Hu notices, and is offended in a quiet, clerkly way.

events.text: Hu's honest report turns up in the archive, under a layer of dust and a newer report that says the opposite. The granary in question has been empty for twenty years. The official who signed the newer report is now the Minister of Revenue.

choices.text: Copy both reports and keep them safe

effects.log: Two reports, one granary, one minister. You sew them into the lining of an old robe.

choices.text: Show them to Hu

effects.log: Hu reads them both, then sits a long time in the cold office with the lamp unlit.

choices.text: Put them back under the dust

effects.log: The archive keeps them, as it has for twenty years. Hu never asks if you found anything.

events.text: Hu retires this spring, with no title and a farewell cup of weak tea. On the last day Hu leaves the good inkstone on your desk, with a note: "For the honest report you will one day write."

choices.text: Send the old reports to the Censorate under your own name

ok.log: The Censorate opens an inquiry. The minister retires "for his health", and Hu's old report is read aloud at court.

fail.log: The Censorate loses your letter. Someone in the Ministry of Revenue does not, and you are passed over that year.

choices.text: Keep the inkstone, and the reports, for a better day

effects.log: You write with Hu's inkstone for the rest of your career. It is still the best one in the office.

choices.text: Visit Hu on the farm with a jar of good tea

effects.log: Hu laughs for the first time in your memory, and tells you which ministers are honest. It is a short list.

events.text: Lamp oil costs three coppers a night, and the Four Books do not read themselves in the dark. Next door, old Widow Tang keeps her lamp lit until midnight for her silkworms, and a crack in the wall lets a thin blade of light fall across your floor.

choices.text: Read by the crack in the wall, crouched on the cold floor

effects.log: You learn the Analects by a sliver of someone else's light. Your back will remember it for years.

choices.text: Offer to feed the widow's silkworms in exchange for a seat by her lamp

effects.log: The silkworms chew all night like soft rain. You read beside them, and Widow Tang pretends not to listen.

choices.text: Buy a whole jar of oil and study properly (30 taels)

effects.log: A whole jar, all yours. For one month you study like the son of a rich house.

events.text: By the second winter Widow Tang can recite the opening of the Great Learning, and corrects you when you skip a line. One night she sets a bowl of millet porridge on your book and says the silkworms have died of the cold, and she cannot afford the oil any more.

choices.text: Give her the last of your savings for oil, for both of you (20 taels)

effects.log: The lamp burns again. The widow says it is for her eyes, not for your exams. It is clearly for your exams.

choices.text: Teach her to read properly, by daylight, in return for porridge

effects.log: By spring she can write her own name and the names of her three dead sons. She frames neither.

choices.text: Move to the temple, where the monks burn lamps for the Buddha all night

effects.log: The temple lamps never go out. The monks charge nothing, and ask only that you stop sighing so loudly.

events.text: On the morning of the county exam, you find a small cloth bundle on your doorstep: two steamed buns, a new brush, and a scrap of paper on which someone has copied, in a shaky hand, the opening of the Great Learning. There is no name.

choices.text: Carry the scrap of paper into the exam hall in your sleeve

effects.log: The guards search you and find it. They read it, laugh, and let you keep it. It is not exactly a cheat sheet.

choices.text: Eat the buns on the way and thank the empty street aloud

effects.log: The street does not answer, but a shutter next door closes very gently.

choices.text: Go next door before the exam to say thank you

effects.log: The widow is asleep at her loom, the lamp burned down to nothing. You leave a copper on the sill and run.

events.text: Years on, a letter reaches you in a careful, shaky hand that you recognise at once. Widow Tang has taught three village girls to read with the lamp you once shared, and the girls want to sit an exam that does not admit girls. She asks, without apology, what you intend to do about it.

choices.text: Send the girls books and a tutor (40 taels)

effects.log: Three girls study by lamplight now, with better oil. One of them writes to you every New Year, in a hand already better than yours.

choices.text: Write back that the world is not fair, but reading still is

effects.log: The widow replies with one line: "Then make it fairer." You keep it pinned above your desk.

choices.text: Visit the old house next door one more time

effects.log: The crack in the wall is still there. Light still falls through it, onto a girl reading on the cold floor.

events.text: A pale young man in the teahouse by the exam hall leans over and whispers a price: fifty taels for this year's county essay question, folded into the filling of a pork dumpling and delivered to your cell on the morning of the exam. He says three candidates have already paid.

choices.text: Pay him and see what you get (50 taels)

effects.log: He gives you a token shaped like a little fish. "Show it to the dumpling seller," he says, and vanishes into the crowd.

choices.text: Note his face, the token, and the teahouse, and walk out

effects.log: You leave your tea half drunk. Behind you the pale young man is already whispering to someone else.

choices.text: Laugh at him: the question is chosen by the magistrate on the morning itself

effects.log: "Not this year," he says, and smiles as if you were a very small child.

events.text: Three days before the exam, the dumpling seller outside the hall is arrested. It turns out the essay questions were real, and so were the dumplings, and the magistrate's own clerk was the cook. The guards are now asking every candidate whether they know anything about little fish tokens.

choices.text: Tell the guards everything you saw at the teahouse

effects.log: Your description of the pale young man is so precise that he is caught at the city gate in a borrowed hat.

choices.text: Throw your fish token into the canal at night

effects.log: The token sinks without a sound. You do not sleep well for a month.

choices.text: Say nothing and keep your head down

effects.log: The guards move along the line of candidates. Their eyes slide over you and stop on the next face.

events.text: The exam is delayed a month, the questions are rewritten by a stern examiner sent from the province, and the whole county studies harder than it ever has. On the morning of the new exam, the dumplings outside the hall are plain pork and very expensive.

choices.text: Sit the exam with only what is in your head

ok.log: You write until your wrist aches, and the essay is honest from the first character to the last. It feels like a good one.

fail.log: The new question is on water control, which you have never studied. You write it anyway, badly, and with great dignity.

choices.text: Buy a dumpling anyway, for luck

effects.log: Plain pork. No paper. You eat it to the last bite and feel strangely clean.

choices.text: Wait outside and watch who else looks nervous

effects.log: Several candidates check their dumplings with their fingers before eating. You recognise two of them from the teahouse.

events.text: Years later, in a provincial town, you are served tea by a pale man in a patched robe who looks at you and freezes. It is the dumpling seller's whisperer, older and thinner, running a teahouse with no exam hall in sight. "I sell only tea now," he says quickly. "Plain tea. No fillings."

choices.text: Drink the tea and leave a generous tip

effects.log: The tea is plain and honest. He watches you go with an expression you cannot name.

choices.text: Ask him who was really behind the ring

effects.log: He looks round the empty room and names a name: the old magistrate's own nephew, now a prefect. You file it away.

choices.text: Tell him you turned him in, if you did

effects.log: He laughs. "Best thing that ever happened to me," he says. "The prison taught me to brew."

events.text: Merchant Qiao, who owns half the salt barges on the river, has a habit: every few years he picks one poor candidate and pays for everything, books, lamp oil, a quiet room, a tutor. This year his steward knocks on your door, looks at your patched robe and your stack of borrowed books, and nods as if buying a horse.

choices.text: Accept the patronage

effects.log: A quiet room above the salt warehouse, a tutor who smells of brine, and more books than you have seen in your life.

choices.text: Ask what the merchant expects in return

effects.log: "Nothing," says the steward, "until you hold a seal." Then he smiles. "After that, everything."

choices.text: Refuse politely: you will rise on your own

effects.log: The steward bows and leaves. By evening the whole street knows you turned down the salt king, and calls you a fool or a saint.

events.text: The tutor is a failed provincial candidate called Master Ou, bitter and brilliant, who drinks plum wine at lunch and corrects your essays in red ink so thick it soaks through the paper. One afternoon he says, quite sober: "Qiao will want a canal permit, in ten years. They always want a canal permit."

choices.text: Ask Ou how the last candidate dealt with Qiao

effects.log: "He became a magistrate," Ou says, "signed the permit, and was hanged for the flood." He pours more wine.

choices.text: Ignore it and keep studying

effects.log: You study harder. The red ink grows a little thinner each month.

choices.text: Leave a polite note and go back to your old room

effects.log: Merchant Qiao sends no reply. Master Ou sends a bottle of plum wine and one word: "Wise."

events.text: Years of study, and the county exam is next spring. Merchant Qiao invites you to a banquet on his biggest barge and introduces you to his guests as "my scholar", the way another man might say "my racehorse". Afterwards he takes your arm and asks, very kindly, whether you have ever thought about canals.

choices.text: Tell Qiao you will owe him gratitude, never a signature

effects.log: Qiao laughs a long time. "Then I have bought an honest scholar," he says. "Those are the rarest. I shall enjoy watching."

choices.text: Promise him anything, with a smile you do not mean

effects.log: Qiao pats your hand. Somewhere a ledger records your name in the column of assets.

choices.text: Repay what he spent on you, with interest, and leave (100 taels)

effects.log: Qiao takes the silver without counting it. "Nobody ever pays me back," he says. "I do not know whether to be pleased."

events.text: Years pass. A flood breaks the dykes on Merchant Qiao's river, and the canal permit he wanted is suddenly at the heart of an inquiry. Old Master Ou, the bitter tutor, sends you a jar of plum wine and a note: "You see? Always a canal. I am glad it is not your name on it."

choices.text: Visit Qiao, ruined and alone on a stranded barge

effects.log: Qiao pours you tea in the wreck of his fortune. "My honest scholar," he says. "The only investment that did not sink."

choices.text: Pour Ou's wine for the tutor's health

effects.log: It smells like terrible wine. You pour it all out for the tutor, and write Ou a long letter about red ink.

choices.text: Send aid to the flooded villages (60 taels)

effects.log: Your silver buys rice for three villages on Qiao's river. The barges carry it free, by Qiao's last order.

events.text: When the county list goes up and your name is on it, the village beats the old drum at the gate, the one kept for floods and weddings. By noon there are thirty people in your yard, a pig you did not order, and an uncle you have never met who says he always believed in you.
events.arc: The Drum at the Village Gate

choices.text: Feast the whole village, and let the pig be eaten

effects.log: The feast lasts until the lanterns burn out. You will be paying for the pig for a year.

choices.text: Thank everyone and go back to your books that same evening

effects.log: The village thinks you are proud. The books think you are wise.

choices.text: Ask the uncle exactly which branch of the family he is from

effects.log: He is from no branch at all. He is a travelling peddler, and he is very good at feasts.

events.text: Passing the county exam means you are now a licentiate, with a scholar's robe and the right not to be beaten by the magistrate. It also means a dozen families want a tutor for their sons, and the village head wants you to write all his letters, for free, forever.
events.arc: The Drum at the Village Gate

choices.text: Tutor the rich families and save for the provincial exam

effects.log: You teach six dull boys and one bright one for a year. The bright one is a cook's boy who listens at the door.

choices.text: Write the village head's letters, all of them

effects.log: Every dispute in the valley now passes through your brush. You learn more law in a year than in ten of study.

choices.text: Refuse it all and study in the hills

effects.log: You rent a hut by a waterfall. The water is loud, the books are many, the village is a little hurt.

events.text: The provincial exam is a month away. You must walk nine days to the provincial capital, sleep in the exam cell for three nights, and come home either a juren or a joke. On the morning you leave, the village gathers at the gate again, more quietly this time.
events.arc: The Drum at the Village Gate

choices.text: Take the cook's boy with you as a servant, and keep teaching him on the road

effects.log: The boy carries your books and recites them back to you on the mountain paths. He is better at it than you were.

choices.text: Promise to beat the drum yourself when you return

effects.log: "If you return a juren," says the village head, "you may beat it all night." The children cheer.

choices.text: Leave before dawn so no one sees you go

effects.log: The road is empty and grey. You hear the drum anyway, once, faintly, as you cross the ridge.

events.text: You come home over the same ridge, whatever the provincial list said. The drum at the village gate is silent. Then the village head appears, a little out of breath, and hands you the drumsticks himself.
events.arc: The Drum at the Village Gate

choices.text: Beat the drum all night, as promised

effects.log: You beat the old drum until the stars go pale. Nobody in the valley sleeps, and nobody complains.

choices.text: Give the drumsticks to the cook's boy

effects.log: The boy beats the drum for both of you, badly and with enormous joy.

choices.text: Hang the drumsticks on your wall, for the next time

effects.log: "Next time," says the village head. The children cheer anyway, at nothing in particular.

events.text: The provincial exam cells are brick boxes with a plank for a desk and a plank for a bed, and they are locked from the outside for three days. On the first night, the candidate in the next cell begins to cough, then to moan, then to talk to someone who is not there.

choices.text: Talk to him through the wall all night, to keep him calm

effects.log: His name is Lu, he is fifty-one, and this is his eleventh provincial exam. By dawn he is calmer than you are.

choices.text: Bang on the door for the guards

effects.log: The guards come, look, and say that a man who leaves his cell fails the exam. Lu begs them to go away.

choices.text: Stuff your ears with cloth and write

effects.log: You write a good essay on the duties of ministers. Through the wall, the moaning goes on all night.

events.text: On the second day Lu falls silent. Then he passes a note through the gap under the wall, in beautiful old-fashioned calligraphy: an essay on frontier granaries, complete, better than anything you have written. "I will not finish," the note says. "Use it."

choices.text: Burn the note and write your own essay

effects.log: The smoke curls up and out through the roof. Your own essay is worse, and entirely yours.

choices.text: Copy a few of its best ideas in your own words

effects.log: You borrow the bones of Lu's essay and dress them in your own clothes. It is a very fine essay now.

choices.text: Slide the note back with one of your own: "Finish it. I will talk you through."

effects.log: For two days you talk through the wall, about rivers and granaries and his wife's noodles. Lu writes.

events.text: The list goes up on a red wall in the provincial capital, and the crowd pushes so hard that a scholar's hat is trampled flat. You find your own name, and then you look for Lu. The eleventh-year hat is nowhere to be seen.

choices.text: Find Lu's name too, near the top, and go to find him

effects.log: Lu is sitting on the steps of the exam hall, weeping into his eleventh-year hat. He buys you noodles, and they are as good as promised.

choices.text: Visit the infirmary where they took Lu

effects.log: He is alive, thin and cheerful. "Twelfth time," he says. "The twelfth is always the lucky one."

choices.text: Wonder all evening whether your essay was yours

effects.log: You passed. The essay on granaries reads well. It reads, if you are honest, a little like Lu.

choices.text: Celebrate with the other new juren

effects.log: The new juren drink until the night watch chases them home. You drink to the empty cell beside yours.

events.text: The palace exam is held in the Hall of Preserving Harmony, and the Son of Heaven sets the question himself. This year it is: "Why did the river provinces starve last winter, when the granaries were full?" Three hundred brushes stop. Everyone knows the answer. Nobody dares to write it.

choices.text: Write the truth: the granaries were full of paper, not rice

effects.log: Your brush shakes only on the first stroke. After that the essay writes itself, and names no names, and names everyone.

choices.text: Write a careful essay about weather, roads and ancient precedents

effects.log: A beautiful essay, perfectly balanced, saying nothing. The examiners will love it.

choices.text: Write the truth, but as a parable about a greedy granary rat

effects.log: Your rat steals the rice, blames the weather, and is promoted. The parable is either very clever or very dangerous.

events.text: The essays go to the Grand Examiner, an old minister named Fang, who is known to be cautious and is also, everyone whispers, a friend of the Minister of Revenue. Two days later Fang summons you to a side room and lays your essay on the table between you.

choices.text: Tell Fang you stand by every word

effects.log: Fang taps the essay. "So do I," he says, very quietly. "Which is why I am putting it in front of the throne, and not in the fire."

choices.text: Ask Fang which ending of the rat story he prefers

effects.log: The old man laughs until he coughs. "The one where the rat is caught," he says. "Let us see if the throne agrees."

choices.text: Bow low and let Fang speak first

effects.log: Fang praises your calligraphy for a long time and your argument not at all. You understand him perfectly.

events.text: The ranking is read aloud at dawn in front of the palace gates. When your name comes, the crier pauses, and adds a line the crowd has never heard before: "The throne has read this essay twice." Then the Minister of Revenue is seen leaving the palace without his hat.

choices.text: Go home and sleep for a day and a night

effects.log: You sleep like a stone. When you wake, there are eleven invitations on the doorstep and one anonymous threat.

choices.text: Send your essay to the river provinces, to be read in the market squares

effects.log: In the river towns, men who starved last winter listen to your essay read aloud, and say your name with something like love.

choices.text: Visit old Fang with a jar of good tea

effects.log: Fang receives you in a plain room with a cold brazier. "I passed thirty years of safe essays," he says. "Thank you for yours."

events.text: Years later a letter comes from the river provinces, signed by forty village heads, thanking you for the essay that refilled their granaries with rice instead of paper. Folded inside is a single grain of rice, wrapped in red paper, as a joke and a promise.

choices.text: Keep the grain of rice on your desk forever

effects.log: Visitors ask why a minister keeps one grain of rice in a jade dish. You tell them, every time.

choices.text: Visit the river provinces to see the granaries yourself

effects.log: The granaries are full. Mostly. You find one with paper in it, and a very surprised official.

choices.text: Write back with a poem about rats

effects.log: The village heads pin your poem to every granary door in the province.

events.text: Everyone in the capital knows the rule: before the palace exam, a candidate pays a call on the examiners. Not a bribe, of course. A courtesy, with a gift. At the gate of Vice Examiner Kong, the gatekeeper looks at your empty hands and says his master is unwell, and will be unwell for some time.

choices.text: Come back with a gift (40 taels)

effects.log: The gatekeeper takes the box and his master recovers instantly. Kong speaks to you about poetry for an hour and about nothing else.

choices.text: Leave your card with a poem on the back instead

effects.log: The poem is about a gatekeeper who guards an empty house. You are rather pleased with it.

choices.text: Do not call on anyone at all

effects.log: You study instead. Other candidates are out every evening in new silk, carrying boxes.

events.text: Kong's gatekeeper finds you in the street a week later, all smiles, and hands you a folded paper. "From my master," he says. "A list of the books the examiners have been reading this spring. Pure coincidence, of course."

choices.text: Read it

effects.log: It is a list of six books. You know three of them. You stay up all week learning the rest.

choices.text: Hand it back unopened

effects.log: The gatekeeper's smile freezes. "My master will be disappointed," he says. You are fairly sure his master will never know.

choices.text: Ask him whether the poem made his master laugh

effects.log: "His master laughed," the gatekeeper says sourly. "The gatekeeper did not."

events.text: At the palace exam itself, Vice Examiner Kong walks the rows of desks, and pauses at yours a moment longer than at the others. He says nothing. A month later, Kong is quietly dismissed for selling lists of books, and every candidate who visited him is questioned.

choices.text: Answer the censors honestly, gift and all

effects.log: The censors note your gift, your honesty and your excellent essay. They seem to weigh all three and let you go.

choices.text: Show them your poem about the empty house

effects.log: The chief censor reads it twice and asks if he may keep it. It goes up on the wall of the Censorate.

choices.text: Wait, worried, for your own summons

effects.log: No summons comes. You never did call on Kong. For once doing nothing was the clever thing.

events.text: New palace graduates are feasted in the Apricot Garden in spring, under trees so full of blossom that petals fall into every cup. A senior official explains the custom: the youngest graduate must climb a tree and pick a branch for the oldest, who this year is a man of sixty-eight called Elder Zhuo.

choices.text: Volunteer to climb, though you are not the youngest

effects.log: You climb, you pick, you come down covered in petals. Elder Zhuo receives the branch as if it were the imperial seal.

choices.text: Sit beside Elder Zhuo and ask about the forty years before this

effects.log: Forty-one exams, he says, one wife, two farms sold, and not one regret. He is lying about the regret, and you both know it.

choices.text: Spend the feast meeting ministers who might want a new clerk

effects.log: You meet four ministers and remember all their names. They remember your face, which is a start.

events.text: Assignments are posted after the feast. Most new graduates go to the Hanlin Academy or a small county far away. Your name is next to a county in the hills where the last two magistrates died of fever, the third of boredom, and the fourth of tigers, according to the clerks.

choices.text: Accept, and set out with a mule and good boots

effects.log: The mule is stubborn, the boots are good, the county is beautiful and very far from anyone who matters.

choices.text: Ask a senior official to look at the list again (60 taels)

effects.log: The list is looked at again. Your name has moved to the Hanlin Academy, where you will copy edicts and be very safe.

choices.text: Ask Elder Zhuo for advice

effects.log: "Go to the hills," he says. "Nobody in the capital ever learned anything." He gives you his apricot branch for luck.

events.text: A year later a letter comes from Elder Zhuo's family, with a dried apricot branch inside: he has died at home, in his garden, with his palace-graduate certificate framed above the bed. The family asks if you would write a few lines for his gravestone.

choices.text: Write the lines: "Forty-one times, and the last was enough"

effects.log: The family carves it in stone. People come from three villages to read it, and the scholars of the county start to sit their exams again.

choices.text: Travel to the funeral yourself

effects.log: The road is long and the funeral is small. The family seats you in the place of honour, next to the framed certificate.

choices.text: Send money for the funeral (40 taels)

effects.log: The family buys a better stone and more incense. Elder Zhuo goes into the hill with music.

events.text: Top Scholar. The title follows you down every street: children chase your sedan, matchmakers line your doorway, and a poem about your hat is sung in the wine shops. Only one man in the capital does not smile when he says it: Ji Hanshu, second on the list by a single mark.

choices.text: Visit Ji with a gift and praise his essay sincerely

effects.log: Ji receives you coldly and reads your card three times. "Sincere," he says at last, as though diagnosing an illness.

choices.text: Ignore him; the list is the list

effects.log: The list is the list. Ji Hanshu has it framed, with your name scratched very faintly with a pin.

choices.text: Read his essay, to see if he should have won

effects.log: It is better than yours in the middle and worse at the end. You were lucky in your ending. You will always know that.

events.text: At the Hanlin Academy, you and Ji Hanshu are given desks side by side, by someone with a sense of humour. Ji works longer hours than anyone. One morning a draft edict you wrote is found to contain a missing character that turns "pardon" into "punish". You did not miss it. Someone took it out.

choices.text: Confront Ji in front of the Academy

effects.log: Ji turns white, then red, and says nothing. The Academy watches, and decides there are two kinds of scholar in the room.

choices.text: Correct the edict quietly and say nothing

effects.log: You fix the character. Ji sees you do it. He does not look up for the rest of the day.

choices.text: Find proof first, then report it

ok.log: The brushstroke that scratched the character is Ji's: he presses on the left. He is sent to a county in the far south.

fail.log: You find nothing. The Academy decides you made the mistake yourself and blamed the runner-up.

events.text: Two years later Ji Hanshu, now a magistrate, is accused of corruption by his own clerks. His family writes to you, of all people, because you are the only famous name they know. The charge, you discover, is false, and the clerks are the ones who stole.

choices.text: Write to the Censorate in Ji's defence

effects.log: Ji is cleared. He writes you one line: "I was second by one mark. I have been second ever since." Then, below it: "Thank you."

choices.text: Defend Ji anyway, though he would not have defended you

effects.log: You defend him. He is cleared. He never writes. Some debts do not like to be paid.

choices.text: Stay out of it

effects.log: Ji is dismissed. You hear he opened a school in the south, where he teaches his students to check every character twice.

events.text: Long years after the list, a book arrives from the south: a textbook for county students, written by Ji Hanshu. The dedication reads "To the one who was first", and the first chapter is about checking every character twice.

choices.text: Use it to teach your own students

effects.log: Your students learn from Ji's textbook, and check every character twice. You never tell them about the edict.

choices.text: Travel south to see Ji's school

effects.log: Ji meets you at the gate, greyer and calmer. You drink tea and agree, at last, that his middle section was better.

choices.text: Write a preface for the second printing

effects.log: Your preface sells the book in every county. Ji writes that he is now second only to his own preface.

events.text: Since the list, everything you write sells. A shopkeeper in the east market is selling scrolls of your calligraphy at twenty taels each, a fair price, except that you have never written any of them. The forger is good: better, if you are honest, on the long downstrokes.

choices.text: Visit the shop in disguise and buy one

effects.log: You pay twenty taels for your own name. The shopkeeper assures you it was written in your presence.

choices.text: Report it to the magistrate

effects.log: The shop is closed and the scrolls are seized. The forger is never found. Prices for your real work double.

choices.text: Laugh it off; it is a compliment

effects.log: The forger works on. Within a year there are more scrolls of yours in the capital than you could write in ten lifetimes.

events.text: The scroll you bought is signed with a tiny mark in the corner: a fishhook. You ask around, and the trail leads to a lane behind the Confucian Temple, where an old man named Wei, who failed the county exam eight times, sits copying famous hands for a living.

choices.text: Offer to buy his whole stock, and his silence

effects.log: Old Wei takes the money and promises to forge only dead men from now on. "They complain less," he says.

choices.text: Sit down and ask him to teach you those downstrokes

effects.log: Wei laughs so hard his brush shakes. Then he shows you, and he is right: you have been doing them wrong all your life.

choices.text: Leave him in peace

effects.log: You go home, sit down, and write a downstroke. It is not as good as Wei's. It is yours.

events.text: The Grand Secretary asks you to write a plaque for the new Hall of Literary Virtue. All the capital will see it; it will hang for a hundred years. You sit down with ink and silk and find that your hand, for the first time in your life, trembles.

choices.text: Ask old Wei to steady the brush beside you

effects.log: Wei holds the silk flat and murmurs "left, now down" at each stroke. The plaque is the best thing you ever write, and only two people know why.

choices.text: Write it alone, trembling and all

effects.log: The plaque is a little uneven on one character. Critics say it shows humility. You say nothing.

choices.text: Decline and recommend an older calligrapher

effects.log: The plaque goes to an old Academician who weeps when he hears. The Grand Secretary thinks you very modest.

events.text: Every tenth day a dozen officials in deliberately plain robes meet at a pavilion over the lotus pond to recite poetry. Everyone knows it is the Pure Stream faction, and that the poems are about eunuchs. Censor Lin, their leader, sends you a card: "We are short of one good rhyme for 'corruption'."
events.arc: The Poetry Club by the Lotus Pond

choices.text: Go, and bring a rhyme

effects.log: Your rhyme is "eruption", which is not elegant but makes old Lin laugh into the lotus. You are invited back.

choices.text: Go, but only listen

effects.log: You hear nine poems about eunuchs, two about frogs, and one about the Emperor's patience, which is the dangerous one.

choices.text: Decline, with a polite poem about being busy

effects.log: Censor Lin pins your refusal to the pavilion pillar. It is quoted there for a month, not kindly.

events.text: At the next meeting a eunuch from the Inner Court rows a small boat past the pavilion, very slowly, feeding the carp. Nobody recites anything. When the boat has gone, Censor Lin produces a memorial accusing Chief Eunuch Gao of selling army posts, already signed by eleven names. There is room for a twelfth.
events.arc: The Poetry Club by the Lotus Pond

choices.text: Sign it

effects.log: Your name goes on the paper beside eleven others. Somewhere across the pond, a carp is very well fed.

choices.text: Ask to see the evidence first

effects.log: Lin shows you ledgers copied from the Ministry of War. They are real, and they are terrible.

choices.text: Excuse yourself and leave by the back gate

effects.log: You walk home through the dark gardens. Behind you the poetry starts again, a little louder.

events.text: The memorial reaches the throne. The Emperor reads it, says nothing for three days, and then sends Chief Eunuch Gao to inspect the southern salt works, very far away, for a very long time. Two of the eleven signers are posted to the frontier the same week.
events.arc: The Poetry Club by the Lotus Pond

choices.text: Ask to be posted to the frontier with them

effects.log: You go west with two poets and a cart of books. Censor Lin sends a poem after you about loyalty, and this time it rhymes.

choices.text: Copy the War Ministry ledgers before they vanish

effects.log: The ledgers vanish the next month. Your copy, sewn into a winter quilt, does not.

choices.text: Celebrate quietly: Gao is gone

effects.log: You raise a cup by the lotus pond. Gao is gone. The eunuch in the boat is still there, feeding the carp.

events.text: Years later Chief Eunuch Gao returns from the salt works, richer and no friendlier, and the Pure Stream poets fall silent one by one. Old Censor Lin is found one morning at the pavilion, gone peacefully in the night with a brush still in hand. The last line on the paper is unfinished.
events.arc: The Poetry Club by the Lotus Pond

choices.text: Finish Lin's line and read it at the funeral

effects.log: You finish it with a rhyme for "corruption". The mourners laugh through their tears, and two eunuchs at the back do not.

choices.text: Send the War Ministry ledgers to the throne at last

effects.log: The ledgers arrive on the Emperor's desk. Gao is sent back to the salt works, and this time he is not given a boat.

choices.text: Keep the paper, and say nothing

effects.log: The unfinished line hangs on your study wall for the rest of your life. Visitors always ask about it.

events.text: A plump, soft-spoken eunuch of the Inner Court, {npc}, stops at your desk in the records office and admires your brushwork. Then {he} invites you to tea in the eunuchs' quarter, which no Pure Stream scholar would be seen dead in, and which serves, everyone admits, the best tea in the palace.

choices.text: Go to tea

effects.log: The tea is from the Emperor's own garden. {npc} talks about nothing at all, very charmingly, for an hour.

choices.text: Decline: clerks who drink with eunuchs do not become ministers

effects.log: {npc} smiles. "Clerks who refuse eunuchs," {he} says, "often do not become anything."

choices.text: Ask {him} what {he} really wants

effects.log: "A friend in the records office," {npc} says simply. "Everyone needs one. Even you."

events.text: A year of teas. {npc} never asks for anything, which is worrying. Then one afternoon {he} mentions, between two sips, that a certain census record from the river provinces would be very interesting to the Inner Court, if it happened to be copied.

choices.text: Copy it for {him}

effects.log: You copy the census. It shows how many people in the river provinces died last winter. {npc} reads it, and for a moment looks very old.

choices.text: Refuse, as a matter of duty

effects.log: {npc} pours more tea. "Duty," {he} says. "Yes. I had that once. It is a good tea for a cold day."

choices.text: Tell the Pure Stream scholars about the request

effects.log: The Pure Stream scholars are delighted. You are now a spy, apparently, for both sides.

events.text: The census records reach the throne by some side door, and the Emperor orders relief grain sent to the river provinces. Whoever sent the records is not named. Then {npc} falls out of favour in a palace quarrel and is sent to tend the imperial tombs in the hills.

choices.text: Visit {npc} at the tombs with good tea

effects.log: {npc} pours the tea on the tomb steps, among the pine needles. "The grain went out," {he} says. "That census was the best thing I ever stole."

choices.text: Send a letter of thanks for all the tea

effects.log: A reply comes, in a fine hand: "You refused me once. It is why I trusted you."

choices.text: Let {npc} go without a word

effects.log: The eunuchs' quarter still serves the best tea in the palace. It tastes of nothing now.

events.text: Word comes from the hills that {npc} has died among the imperial tombs, peacefully, in a small house full of tea jars. A box arrives with your name on it in a fine hand: the best tea from the eunuchs' quarter, and a list of every honest official {npc} ever helped in secret. Yours is the last name.

choices.text: Read the whole list

effects.npcPass: old age, among the imperial tombs
effects.log: Thirty names, over forty years. Several are famous for their honesty, and none of them ever knew.

choices.text: Brew the tea at {npc}'s grave

effects.npcPass: old age, among the imperial tombs
effects.log: You brew it on the hillside among the pines. It is the best tea in the empire, still.

choices.text: Give the tea to the eunuchs' quarter, in {npc}'s name

effects.npcPass: old age, among the imperial tombs
effects.log: The old eunuchs drink to {npc}'s memory, and one of them weeps into the cup.

events.text: The new canal tax has emptied the boatmen's villages along the Grand Canal: whole families walking north with their pots tied to their backs. Your seal gives you the right to submit a memorial straight to the throne. You also know the tax was the Emperor's own idea, written in his own brush.
events.arc: A Memorial on the Canal Tax

choices.text: Draft a blunt memorial: the tax must go

effects.log: You write all night. By dawn the memorial is short, true, and quite possibly the end of your career.

choices.text: Draft a gentle memorial praising the tax, then proposing exceptions

effects.log: Your memorial praises the Emperor's wisdom for nine pages and asks for mercy on the tenth.

choices.text: Do nothing; the tax is not your office's business

effects.log: The boatmen keep walking north. Your office's business remains in excellent order.

events.text: Before you can submit it, the Chancellor's secretary visits your home. The Chancellor, he says, has heard about a certain memorial, and would like you to know that ministers who embarrass the throne sometimes find themselves inspecting the frontier latrines. He leaves a box of good ginseng on the way out.
events.arc: A Memorial on the Canal Tax

choices.text: Return the ginseng and submit the memorial anyway

effects.log: The ginseng goes back unopened. The memorial goes into the throne room on a lacquer tray the next morning.

choices.text: Show the Chancellor your draft first, to win him over

effects.log: The Chancellor reads it, sighs, and crosses out one line. Then he signs his own name under yours.

choices.text: Keep the ginseng and burn the memorial

effects.log: The ginseng is excellent. You feel very healthy and very small.

events.text: The throne room is silent while the Emperor reads. He reads it twice. Then he lays it down and asks, in a voice that carries to the back of the hall, which minister wrote this. Three hundred officials study the floor tiles with great interest.
events.arc: A Memorial on the Canal Tax

choices.text: Step forward

effects.log: "You have courage," the Emperor says, "and I have a headache." The tax is halved by the end of the month, and you are not thanked.

choices.text: Step forward and argue for abolishing it entirely

ok.log: You speak for the boatmen until the incense burns down. The tax is abolished, and the boatmen's songs about you are sung on the canal for a generation.

fail.log: The Emperor stops you halfway. "Enough." The tax stays, and you are sent to count barges on the canal for a year.

choices.text: Let the Chancellor speak for both of you

effects.log: The Chancellor speaks softly and long. The tax is suspended in three provinces, and the Chancellor takes most of the credit.

events.text: Years later, boatmen on the Grand Canal still sing about the minister who knelt for them. You hear it yourself one evening from a passing barge, wrong in every detail and right in the only one that matters.
events.arc: A Memorial on the Canal Tax

choices.text: Call out to the barge and correct the details

effects.log: The boatmen laugh and invite you aboard. By the end of the night the song has a new verse, worse than the old ones.

choices.text: Listen in silence until the barge is gone

effects.log: The song fades down the water. You stand on the bank for a long time.

choices.text: Ride the canal to see the villages again

effects.log: The villages are full of people and pots again. Nobody recognises you, which is exactly right.

events.text: A junior censor named {npc} has impeached you. The charges: arriving late to the dawn audience twice, owning a hat with an improper number of tassels, and "an air of private satisfaction unbecoming to a servant of the throne". The whole court thinks it is a joke. {npc} does not.
events.arc: The Censor Who Hates Your Hat

choices.text: Answer every charge in writing, with precedents

effects.log: Your reply runs to forty pages and cites a ruling from three dynasties ago about tassels. {npc} reads all of it.

choices.text: Invite {npc} to dinner

effects.log: {npc} accepts, eats very little, and studies your house the whole evening as if counting the roof tiles.

choices.text: Ignore it; a censor's paper is only paper

effects.log: The impeachment sits in a drawer at the Censorate. So, you later learn, does a much thicker file.

events.text: {npc} has been asking questions about the timber for the new ministry roof. Your steward bought it; your steward is your cook's cousin's nephew, more or less; and the price was three times the market rate. You did not know. {npc} does not believe that.
events.arc: The Censor Who Hates Your Hat

choices.text: Go through the accounts yourself and find out

effects.log: The steward has been skimming for years. Most of the money went to gambling debts and one very expensive cricket.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to look through the accounts with you

effects.log: Two nights in a cold office. {npc} finds the theft first, and seems almost disappointed that you were not part of it.

choices.text: Pay back the difference from your own pocket (120 taels)

effects.log: The roof is paid for twice. {npc} notes the payment in the file, under the heading "guilt?"

events.text: The hearing is held at the Censorate. {npc} presents the case well, with the timber, the hat and the air of private satisfaction. Then {he} turns to you and, unexpectedly, asks you to speak for yourself without notes.
events.arc: The Censor Who Hates Your Hat

choices.text: Hand over the steward and the proof

effects.log: The steward is dismissed and the timber case collapses. {npc} withdraws the charges and keeps the one about the hat, on principle.

choices.text: Admit your carelessness and ask for a fine, not a pardon

effects.log: The Censorate fines you a month's salary. {npc} nods once, as if you have passed a test nobody told you about.

choices.text: Argue that tassels are a matter of taste, not law

ok.log: The hall laughs. Even {npc} smiles, very slightly. The charges are dropped, and you wear the hat the next day.

fail.log: Nobody laughs. You are demoted half a grade and the hat is confiscated.

events.text: Years pass. {npc} becomes Chief Censor, still poor, still impeaching ministers for their hats. When you fall ill one winter, a pot of chicken broth arrives at your gate with no name, and a note: "Tassels still improper. Get well."
events.arc: The Censor Who Hates Your Hat

choices.text: Send back a tassel, with your thanks

effects.log: {npc} keeps the tassel on the Censorate desk. Ministers who visit are told it is evidence.

choices.text: Recommend {npc} to the throne for the Order of the Upright Brush

effects.log: The award is given. {npc} wears it once, to impeach the official who presents it.

choices.text: Drink the broth and laugh until you cough

effects.log: It is very good broth. You recover by spring, with an air of private satisfaction.

events.text: A land dispute between two families in Plum Village has reached your yamen: the Zhangs say the Lius moved a boundary stone; the Lius say the stone moved itself. The next morning a basket of melons arrives from the Zhangs. Under the melons, wrapped in red paper, are two hundred taels.

choices.text: Return everything, melons included

effects.log: The basket goes back up the road on a donkey. The Zhang patriarch is said to have wept with frustration.

choices.text: Keep the melons, return the silver

effects.log: The melons are excellent. The silver goes back with a note: "The stone will be judged by the stone."

choices.text: Keep it all

effects.log: The Lius' basket arrives an hour later. It contains three hundred taels and no melons, which you find insulting.

events.text: You ride out to Plum Village to see the boundary stone for yourself. It is a grey lump in a field of beans, with fresh scratches around its base and goat droppings on top. An old goat is tethered nearby, chewing with great satisfaction, belonging to neither family.

choices.text: Question the goat's owner

effects.log: The goat belongs to a widow who swears it pushes the stone every spring, looking for the sweet grass underneath. Both families stare at the goat.

choices.text: Measure the field against the county register

effects.log: The register says the stone has moved half a pace. Nobody is surprised. Everybody is guilty.

choices.text: Rule now, in the field, by your own judgment

effects.log: You split the strip in half. Both families are furious, which in your experience means it was fair.

events.text: The verdict is read at the yamen gate to half the village. Whatever you rule, a basket of melons will stand between these two families for a generation. The goat, tethered by the gate, has come to watch.

choices.text: Rule that the goat is to blame, and fine it one melon a year

effects.log: The village roars with laughter. The goat is fined, both families pay, and they share the melon every autumn.

choices.text: Rule for the Lius, and send the Zhangs' bribe to the county school

effects.log: The Zhangs are humiliated, the Lius delighted, and the county school gets new roof tiles.

choices.text: Rule for whoever paid more

effects.log: The Lius win. Plum Village decides exactly what kind of official you are, and sings a song about it.

choices.text: Fix the stone in place with mortar, at the county's cost

effects.log: Mortar and a new stone, and a line in the register. The goat is disappointed.

events.text: A few years on, a cart arrives at your gate from Plum Village: a basket of melons, nothing underneath, from the Zhangs and the Lius together. The two families have married a son to a daughter, and the boundary stone stands in the middle of their joint field, with the old goat tethered to it.

choices.text: Eat the melons and send a wedding gift

effects.log: The melons are the best you have ever had. Your gift is a small brass bell for the goat.

choices.text: Search the basket anyway, out of habit

effects.log: Nothing but melons. And, at the very bottom, a child's drawing of a goat wearing an official's hat.

choices.text: Ride to Plum Village for the wedding

effects.log: You are given the seat of honour, between the two patriarchs and directly downwind of the goat.

events.text: {npc} of the Censorate is famous for owning one robe, eating rice with pickles, and impeaching anyone. Today {he} stands at your door in the rain with a memorial against the Governor of Huai province and asks you, of all the court, to add your name. "You are honest," {npc} says, "or at least not yet bought."
events.arc: The Censor Who Owns One Robe

choices.text: Invite {him} in and read it

effects.log: The memorial is precise, furious and well-sourced. {npc} drinks your tea as if it were a luxury, which for {him} it is.

choices.text: Sign without reading; the name {npc} is enough

effects.log: {npc} looks at you sharply. "Never do that again," {he} says, "not even for me." But {he} takes the signature.

choices.text: Refuse; the Governor is the Chancellor's cousin

effects.log: {npc} bows and walks away into the rain. You watch the one robe get wetter until the corner turns.

events.text: The Governor's men come to the capital. Small accidents follow {npc}: a rock through the window, a cart that nearly runs {him} down, a rumour about bribes so absurd that even the Governor's friends are embarrassed. {npc} keeps walking to work in the one robe.
events.arc: The Censor Who Owns One Robe

choices.text: Sign the memorial now, having read it

effects.log: Your name goes down. Two more ministers sign the next day, because if you dared, they can.

choices.text: Give {npc} a guard from your own household

effects.log: {npc} refuses the guard, then accepts a large umbrella. The guard follows anyway, at a respectful distance.

choices.text: Buy {him} a second robe (20 taels)

effects.log: {npc} is deeply suspicious of the second robe, and wears it only to funerals.

events.text: The memorial reaches the throne. An inquiry sent to Huai finds granaries full of sand and a Governor's house full of jade. The Governor is dismissed. {npc} goes home that evening, eats rice with pickles, and is back at the Censorate at dawn.
events.arc: The Censor Who Owns One Robe

choices.text: Celebrate with {npc} over rice and pickles

effects.log: The pickles are very sour. {npc} laughs for the first time in your acquaintance, and the sound is rusty.

choices.text: Accept the throne's thanks for your signature

effects.log: The Emperor sends you a jade seal from the Governor's own house. It is very fine, and slightly awkward.

choices.text: Write the inquiry's findings up for the court gazette

effects.log: Every county in the empire reads about the sand in Huai's granaries. Several governors check their own.

events.text: {npc} retires at last, as poor as the day {he} started, and the Censorate gives a farewell banquet {he} refuses to attend. Instead {npc} sends you a parcel: the one robe, washed and folded, with a note: "For the next honest fool. You will know who."
events.arc: The Censor Who Owns One Robe

choices.text: Give the robe to the most stubborn young censor you know

effects.log: The young censor wears it to court the next day and impeaches a vice minister by noon. It fits.

choices.text: Visit {npc} with rice and pickles

effects.log: You find {npc} in a tiny house with a big garden, impeaching the cabbages for laziness.

choices.text: Keep the robe in your own wardrobe

effects.log: You never wear it, but you look at it every morning before you dress for court.

events.text: The post of Minister of Rites is vacant, and the court will vote. The Pure Stream scholars want old Academician Xu, who is honest and deaf. The Inner Court eunuchs want Vice Minister Hong, who is clever and theirs. Both sides have counted their votes, and both have found that yours decides it.

choices.text: Promise your vote to Xu

effects.log: Within an hour, three Pure Stream poets have written verses in your honour, and the eunuchs have stopped greeting you in the corridors.

choices.text: Promise your vote to Hong

effects.log: A eunuch you have never met sends you a jar of lychees from the Emperor's own orchard. The Pure Stream poets write a different kind of verse.

choices.text: Promise nothing to anyone

effects.log: Both factions double their efforts. Your doorstep becomes the busiest in the capital.

events.text: Three nights before the vote, both candidates visit you, separately, in disguise. Old Xu cannot hear your greeting and talks for an hour about ritual music. Hong arrives an hour later, listens to every word, and offers you, without blinking, the Ministry of Personnel.

choices.text: Ask Hong what the Inner Court wants from the Ministry of Rites

effects.log: "The calendar," Hong says. "Who chooses the lucky days, chooses everything." You never forget it.

choices.text: Suggest a third candidate: Xu's clever student Shen

effects.log: Both factions are horrified. Then both slowly realise that Shen might be the only person neither side can control.

choices.text: Hear them both and sleep on it

effects.log: You sleep badly, dreaming of ritual music and lychees.

events.text: The court votes at dawn, one name at a time, in the Hall of Supreme Harmony. When it is your turn, the hall goes so silent that you can hear a eunuch's sleeve rustle. Old Xu, in the front row, is cupping one ear.

choices.text: Vote for old Xu

effects.log: Xu wins, and does not hear the result. When told, he bows to the wrong side of the hall. The Pure Stream are triumphant.

choices.text: Vote for Hong

effects.log: Hong wins and the Inner Court controls the calendar. Your next three years are very lucky, on paper.

choices.text: Vote for Shen, and watch the hall split

effects.log: Shen wins by one vote: yours. Neither faction thanks you, and both now fear you a little.

choices.text: Abstain, and warn the throne about the calendar

effects.log: The throne thanks you privately and moves the calendar to the Imperial Observatory. Both factions lose. Both blame you.

events.text: Years later the vote for the Minister of Rites is still remembered at court as the night the hall went silent. Young officials ask you about it as if it were history. Both factions, you notice, still count your vote first.

choices.text: Tell the young officials to vote by conscience

effects.log: They nod and go away and vote by faction. One or two, you hope, remember.

choices.text: Tell them about the calendar, and who chooses lucky days

effects.log: The young officials go pale. You have taught them more about the court in an hour than the Academy did in years.

choices.text: Tell them nothing and smile

effects.log: Your smile becomes famous. Nobody knows what it means, which is its whole use.

events.text: {npc}, Minister of War, has opposed every proposal you have made for two years: grain, roads, even the colour of the new examination paper. Today {npc} invites you to see {his} famous rock garden, and you cannot think of a polite reason to refuse.

choices.text: Go, and praise the rocks honestly

effects.log: The rocks are magnificent. {npc} seems almost hurt that you like them.

choices.text: Go, and bring a rock of your own as a gift

effects.log: Your rock is small and ugly and came from the bottom of your own pond. {npc} looks at it for a long time, then puts it in the middle of the garden.

choices.text: Send a gift and stay home

effects.log: The gift is returned with a note: "Rocks are for people who have the time to look at them."

events.text: Walking among the rocks, {npc} speaks at last. The war on the frontier is going badly, worse than the court knows, and the reports are being softened before they reach the throne. {npc} has opposed you, {he} says, because you are the only one at court the throne still listens to, and {he} did not trust you.

choices.text: Ask {him} for the true reports

effects.log: {npc} hands you a bundle from inside a hollow rock. They are worse than you imagined.

choices.text: Ask why {he} should trust you now

effects.log: "Because you came," {npc} says. "My enemies never come to see my rocks."

choices.text: Leave; this is a trap

effects.log: You leave the garden at a brisk walk. {npc} watches you go without a word, and opposes your next proposal as usual.

events.text: At the next audience you must decide what to do with what {npc} told you. The Chancellor, who softened the reports, is standing three paces from the throne, smiling. {npc} stands across the hall, not looking at you at all.

choices.text: Read the true reports aloud before the throne

effects.log: The hall goes silent. The Chancellor stops smiling. Reinforcements march for the frontier within the week.

choices.text: Propose a joint inspection with {npc} of the frontier

effects.log: You and your old rival ride west together for a month and argue about everything. The reports are never softened again.

choices.text: Say nothing in court, but warn the throne privately

effects.log: The Emperor listens, frowns, and asks why the Minister of War did not come in person. You have no good answer.

events.text: {npc} retires from the Ministry of War and sends you a cart. On it sits one rock: the small ugly one from the bottom of your pond, or one very like it, with a line carved on the base: "The only honest stone in my garden."

choices.text: Put it back in your pond

effects.log: The rock goes home to the bottom of your pond. You visit it more than you expected to.

choices.text: Visit {npc} in retirement

effects.log: You find {npc} in a much smaller garden with much smaller rocks, opposing the neighbours' choice of fence.

choices.text: Send {npc} a rock in return, the largest you can find (30 taels)

effects.log: Eight oxen deliver it. {npc} writes that it is vulgar and has placed it in the centre of the garden.

events.text: The Emperor is in a fury: the floods have broken the dykes in three provinces, and the minister reporting it has just admitted that the dyke money was spent on a new palace pavilion. An inkstone flies across the hall and lands, by pure bad luck, at your feet.

choices.text: Pick it up and return it with both hands, kneeling

effects.log: The Emperor stares at you, then at the inkstone, then sits down. The storm passes over the hall like a cloud.

choices.text: Leave it where it lies and keep your head down

effects.log: The inkstone lies on the floor for the rest of the audience. Nobody dares to pick it up. It is still there at sunset.

choices.text: Speak up: the dykes must be repaired today, whatever it costs

effects.log: Every head turns. The Emperor glares at you, and then says: "Then you do it."

events.text: Whether you asked for it or not, the dyke repairs are now partly your affair. The provinces need forty thousand labourers and the treasury is empty. The Minister of Works, who spent the money on the pavilion, sends you an anxious note offering to help.

choices.text: Order the pavilion's timber and stone taken for the dykes

effects.log: The pavilion comes down a beam at a time and goes down the river on barges. The Minister of Works watches from his window.

choices.text: Ask the rich salt merchants for a loan, against future taxes

effects.log: The merchants lend, at interest that will be paid for twenty years. The dykes go up before the spring floods.

choices.text: Accept the Minister's help, and watch him closely

effects.log: The Minister works like a man possessed, in mud to the knees. Guilt is a fine foreman.

events.text: By spring the dykes hold. The Emperor sends you, by a eunuch's hand, the same inkstone that flew across the hall, now set in a sandalwood box with a single line in the imperial brush: "For the one who caught it."

choices.text: Use it every day

effects.log: You write every report on the flying inkstone. Your colleagues treat your desk like a shrine.

choices.text: Give it to the dyke labourers' shrine on the river

effects.log: The labourers put the Emperor's inkstone on the shrine of the river god. It is very much admired by both.

choices.text: Keep it in its box, unused, for safety

effects.log: The inkstone sits in its box, unused and perfect. It is a very safe inkstone.

events.text: The Emperor is bored. He has yawned through three audiences, sent away two concubines and a juggler, and today announced that the next official to bore him will be posted to the southern border. Then he asks, of the whole court, whether anyone has a fighting cricket worth watching.

choices.text: Say you know a famous cricket keeper in the south market

effects.log: The Emperor sits up. "Bring them," he says. You now have three days to find a famous cricket keeper.

choices.text: Suggest a debate on the classics instead

effects.log: The Emperor gives you a long, long look. You are not sent south, but it is close.

choices.text: Stay silent and let someone else be brave

effects.log: A eunuch volunteers his own cricket. It loses to a palace cat. The court is very, very quiet.

events.text: Cricket fever sweeps the palace. Ministers who could not name the Five Classics can now name every champion cricket in the capital. Prices climb: a good fighter costs as much as a horse. In the south market, a boy named Ninth Wang has a cricket called Iron General that has never lost.

choices.text: Buy Iron General for the Emperor (80 taels)

effects.log: Ninth Wang counts the silver three times and weeps for his cricket. Iron General is carried to the palace in a jade cage.

choices.text: Bring Ninth Wang and the cricket together, as keeper

effects.log: The boy is washed, dressed in silk and taken to the palace, still clutching his cricket. He is not impressed by the palace.

choices.text: Write a memorial: the court has forgotten the provinces

effects.log: The memorial is read, set aside, and used by a eunuch to line a cricket box.

events.text: Iron General faces the Chancellor's champion before the whole court. The Emperor leans so far forward that his crown slips. Whatever happens next, it will be talked about in every teahouse in the empire.

choices.text: Coach Iron General with a straw, as Ninth Wang taught you

ok.log: Iron General wins in three charges. The Emperor laughs aloud for the first time in a year, and makes Ninth Wang an Imperial Cricket Keeper.

fail.log: Iron General walks out of the ring and refuses to return. The Emperor laughs anyway, which is somehow worse.

choices.text: Bow and ask that the winner's prize go to the flood provinces

effects.log: The Emperor, in a good mood, agrees. A cricket fight feeds a county for a winter.

choices.text: Watch, cheer, and say nothing clever

effects.log: You cheer for the Chancellor's cricket. The Chancellor remembers it fondly.

events.text: A comet hangs over the capital, a long pale broom sweeping the stars. The Emperor has not slept in three nights. The Imperial Astrologer says a broom star means the throne must sweep away a wicked minister, and everyone at court is very carefully not looking at everyone else.

choices.text: Read the old records of comets in the archives

effects.log: Twelve comets in five hundred years. After four of them a minister was executed. After the other eight, nothing happened at all.

choices.text: Ask the Astrologer which minister the stars mean

effects.log: The Astrologer smiles and says the stars will tell him tomorrow. You suspect the stars will be told what to say tonight.

choices.text: Keep your head down and your record clean

effects.log: You check your accounts twice. Every minister in the capital does the same.

events.text: The Astrologer names a name: old Minister Pei of the Board of Works, who has spent ten years refusing to approve a new palace for the Empress Dowager's eunuchs. Pei is arrested at dawn. The comet, unconcerned, goes on sweeping.

choices.text: Present the comet records to the throne

effects.log: The Emperor reads them and asks the Astrologer, very quietly, why only four of the twelve comets were wicked.

choices.text: Visit Pei in prison with a quilt and a book

effects.log: Pei is cheerful. "A comet," he says. "I have been brought down by the sky. It is almost an honour."

choices.text: Say nothing: the sky has spoken

effects.log: The sky has spoken. You are not sure it said this.

events.text: The comet fades. The Emperor, rested at last, begins to wonder why the stars wanted a palace for the eunuchs. Minister Pei's fate is still undecided, and the Astrologer has taken a sudden interest in travel.

choices.text: Speak for Pei's release at the audience

effects.log: Pei is released and restored to his post. On his first day back, he refuses the eunuchs' palace again.

choices.text: Ask that the Astrologer be given time to study the sky more carefully, far away

effects.log: The Astrologer is sent to a mountain observatory near the steppe. The stars are very clear there, and very cold.

choices.text: Write a short treatise: comets are only comets

effects.log: The treatise is banned in the palace and copied in every teahouse. Nobody is executed for the next comet.

events.text: Some years later another comet appears, smaller and dimmer. The court holds its breath. The Emperor, at the morning audience, asks only one question: "Has anyone checked the archives?" Every head in the hall turns toward you.

choices.text: Present the records again, with one more comet added

effects.log: Thirteen comets now, and still only four ministers. The Emperor nods and goes back to the grain reports.

choices.text: Suggest the Astrologer be asked for an opinion, from the mountains

effects.log: A letter from the cold observatory arrives a month later: "It is a comet." The court finds this very reassuring.

choices.text: Say the sky is busy and the court has work to do

effects.log: The audience moves on. Nobody is arrested. The comet passes like a cat across a roof.

events.text: The Emperor is generous today. A good harvest, a new grandson, a favourable report: he is giving gifts to everyone in sight. A eunuch arrives at your desk with ten bolts of imperial yellow silk and a deed to a house near the Drum Tower. Your colleagues receive nothing at all.

choices.text: Accept humbly and share the silk among the office

effects.log: Ten bolts become forty robes. The office is the best-dressed in the palace, and suddenly very fond of you.

choices.text: Accept everything and move into the house

effects.log: The house has a garden, a well and a gatekeeper who has served six previous owners. All six, he mentions, fell from favour.

choices.text: Ask the eunuch why you, and why today

effects.log: "The Emperor saw your face in the corridor," the eunuch says, "and liked it." That is all there is.

events.text: Envy is a quiet animal at court. Within a month you have three new enemies, one anonymous poem about unearned favour, and a request from the Chancellor's nephew to borrow your new house for a banquet, indefinitely.

choices.text: Lend the house to the nephew

effects.log: The nephew's banquet lasts four months. The Chancellor is very grateful. Your garden is not.

choices.text: Answer the poem with a better poem

effects.log: Your poem is about a magpie who is given a golden cage and promptly sells it. It is much quoted.

choices.text: Work twice as hard, to earn it afterwards

effects.log: You work every night for a year. The envy fades. Your eyesight does too, a little.

events.text: Favour turns like weather. The Emperor's mood shifts, and gifts are being quietly taken back from half the court. A eunuch appears at your door with a polite list, a brush and a cart, and an expression of deep regret.

choices.text: Return the house before it is asked for

effects.log: The eunuch is so surprised he forgets his speech. The Emperor hears of it, and does not take back the silk.

choices.text: Return nothing: a gift is a gift

effects.log: The list is read aloud at your gate. You lose the house, and the street gains a story.

choices.text: Show the eunuch the forty robes, already worn

effects.log: The eunuch looks at forty clerks in imperial yellow and gives up. Some gifts cannot be taken back.

events.text: The Emperor's beloved consort has died in childbirth, and the child with her. The court wears white for a hundred days. The Emperor has stopped attending audiences, and the empire waits for decisions that only he can make: a drought in the west, a border treaty, a new governor for the south.

choices.text: Keep the ministries running, quietly, without the throne

effects.log: You sign what can be signed and hold back what cannot. The empire limps on, and nobody calls it a regency.

choices.text: Request an audience to speak to him as one person to another

effects.log: The audience is refused. Then, at midnight, a eunuch comes for you with a lantern.

choices.text: Wait, like everyone else

effects.log: Everyone waits. The drought in the west does not.

events.text: The Emperor sits in the consort's garden among the plum trees she planted. He does not look up. "They tell me the west is dry," he says. "She was from the west. Did you know that?"

choices.text: Tell him the west needs him, the way she did

effects.log: The Emperor is silent for a long time. Then he asks for the drought reports, and reads them by lantern light in her garden.

choices.text: Say nothing and sit with him until dawn

effects.log: You sit among the plum trees until the sky goes grey. Neither of you says a word. It is the most important audience of your career.

choices.text: Bring him the sealed decisions to sign, gently

effects.log: He signs every one without reading. The decisions are good. He knows they are, because you made them.

events.text: On the hundredth day the white robes come off. The Emperor returns to the throne, thinner and older, and the first thing he does is order a canal dug in the west, named for the consort, to carry water to her home province.

choices.text: Volunteer to oversee the canal

effects.log: You spend three years in the dust of the west. When the water comes through, the villagers burn incense for the consort and, quietly, for you.

choices.text: Write the inscription for the canal stone

effects.log: The inscription is short. The Emperor reads it, says nothing, and has it carved exactly as written.

choices.text: Return to your office and the ordinary work

effects.log: The ordinary work is waiting. It always is. You find it a comfort.

events.text: Your cousin {ct_plotter} has taken up archery. So have three hundred of his household guards, who practise every morning in a field outside the capital, and so, your spies report, have two generals who dine at his house every tenth day. {ct_plotter} sends you a gift: a beautiful bow.

choices.text: Thank {ct_plotter} warmly, and double the palace guard

effects.log: The palace guard doubles quietly. {ct_plotter} sends a second bow, which is either a joke or a message.

choices.text: Invite {ct_plotter} to an archery contest at the palace

effects.log: The prince accepts with a smile that shows every tooth. The whole court is suddenly very interested in archery.

choices.text: Send the two generals to the far frontier, with promotions

effects.log: The generals go west with new titles and long faces. {ct_plotter} writes that he will miss their company.

events.text: A eunuch brings you a letter in {ct_plotter}'s hand, intercepted on its way to the northern garrison. It speaks of "the autumn hunt" and "the great stag" in terms too careful to be about deer. You are, as everyone knows, going on the autumn hunt.

choices.text: Cancel the hunt, citing a sore back

effects.log: The hunt is cancelled. {ct_plotter} sends his sympathies and a jar of tiger-bone ointment, which you have tested by a physician.

choices.text: Go on the hunt, with the doubled guard disguised as beaters

effects.log: You ride out to the hunt with three hundred very alert beaters. Not a single stag dares to appear.

choices.text: Show the letter to {ct_plotter}'s own mother, the Dowager Consort

effects.log: The old woman reads it, goes white, and asks for one night. In the morning, the prince is ill and cannot hunt.

events.text: Whatever was planned for the autumn did not happen. {ct_plotter} kneels in the throne room now, in plain robes, among his own bows, and waits to hear what the Son of Heaven will do with a cousin.

choices.text: Exile him to a distant fief, with his bows

effects.log: {ct_plotter} goes south to a fief with fine hunting and no army. He writes you a poem every New Year, each one more bitter.

choices.text: Pardon him publicly, and keep him at court where you can see him

effects.log: The court thinks you either weak or very clever. {ct_plotter} thinks so too, and does not sleep well for a year.

choices.text: Strip him of rank and confine him to a monastery

effects.log: The prince becomes a monk with very good aim. The monastery's archery is said to be the best in the empire.

choices.text: Make him Grand Marshal of the frontier, far from the capital

effects.log: "You wanted an army," you tell him. "Here is one, and a steppe to point it at." He goes, astonished.

events.text: Years pass. A letter comes from {ct_plotter}, older now, asking permission to return to the capital for his mother's funeral. The court is divided: some say it is a trick, some say it is grief, and some say it can be both.

choices.text: Let him come, and walk beside him in the procession

effects.log: The two of you walk behind the Dowager Consort's coffin side by side. Whatever he planned once, today he only weeps.

choices.text: Let him come, under guard

effects.log: The prince arrives between two lines of guards and bows to you very correctly. Nobody can tell what he feels.

choices.text: Refuse, and send rich gifts to the funeral instead

effects.log: The gifts arrive. The prince keeps them, and writes no more poems.

events.text: Old Grand Tutor Ruan taught you the classics when you were small, with a bamboo rod and no fear of rank. He is ninety now, and has asked for an audience. He walks into the throne room with a cane, does not kneel, and says your last edict had three grammatical errors.

choices.text: Thank him and have the edict reissued, corrected

effects.log: The edict is reissued. The whole court learns that the Son of Heaven can be corrected, and some of them begin to try.

choices.text: Laugh, and give him a chair beside the throne

effects.log: Ruan sits beside the throne for the rest of the audience, muttering at every minister. It is the best audience in years.

choices.text: Remind him, kindly, that you are no longer his pupil

effects.log: Ruan looks at you for a long moment. "No," he says. "I suppose not." He leaves, and does not ask again.

events.text: Ruan has a second complaint, and this time he waits until the hall is empty. The new tax on salt, he says, is making the price of pickled vegetables impossible in the villages. "You never ate pickles," he says. "Most of your people eat nothing else."

choices.text: Order the salt tax reviewed

effects.log: The tax is reviewed and lowered. In the villages the pickle jars are full again, and nobody knows why.

choices.text: Ask Ruan to take you, in disguise, to a village market

effects.log: You walk through a market in plain cotton beside your old tutor. You buy pickles. They cost far too much.

choices.text: Tell him the treasury needs the salt money for the frontier

effects.log: "Then the frontier is eating the villages' pickles," Ruan says. "Write that in the edict, with correct grammar."

events.text: Grand Tutor Ruan dies in his sleep that winter, with a half-corrected essay of yours from forty years ago on his desk. The red ink is still wet on a character you always got wrong.

choices.text: Finish correcting the essay yourself, and bury it with him

effects.log: You correct the character. It takes you three tries. Ruan goes into the ground with his last lesson finished.

choices.text: Order a day of mourning in every village school

effects.log: Every village school in the empire closes for a day, and every child is told about a tutor who scolded an emperor.

choices.text: Go to the village market again, alone, and buy pickles

effects.log: The pickles are cheaper now. You eat them on the temple steps where nobody knows you, and you weep a little.

events.text: A white crane lands on the roof of the Hall of Supreme Harmony and refuses to leave. The Board of Rites declares it an omen of a sage ruler. The Imperial Astrologer declares it an omen of a drought. The cooks declare it is eating the palace koi.
events.arc: The White Crane Over the Palace

choices.text: Accept the Board of Rites' reading and order celebrations

effects.log: Lanterns, fireworks, a poem in every village. The crane is unimpressed and eats another koi.

choices.text: Ask the Astrologer to explain the drought

effects.log: The Astrologer explains at length. You understand that he has been paid by a grain merchant who would like grain prices to rise.

choices.text: Ask the cooks to put a net over the koi pond

effects.log: The net goes up. The crane looks at the net, at you, and then flies off to the Chancellor's garden. Omens are fickle.

events.text: The crane has been followed by petitioners: a farmer who says it cured his blind ox, a monk who wants to build a temple on the spot, and a delegation of ministers who propose renaming the reign era "Auspicious Crane". The crane has now settled on the palace granary.
events.arc: The White Crane Over the Palace

choices.text: Rename the era: let the people have their omen

effects.log: The "Auspicious Crane" era begins. Crane-shaped buns sell out in every market in the capital.

choices.text: Arrest the grain merchant who paid the Astrologer

effects.log: The merchant's warehouses are found to hold a year's grain bought up in secret. Prices fall at once.

choices.text: Refuse every petition: a bird is a bird

effects.log: The ministers are disappointed. The farmer's ox stays cured anyway.

events.text: One morning the crane is gone, flown north. The court waits to see what the Son of Heaven will make of its leaving, because an omen that departs is still an omen, and every faction has its reading ready.
events.arc: The White Crane Over the Palace

choices.text: Declare that the crane has gone to bless the frontier

effects.log: The frontier garrisons hear that the sacred crane flew their way. Morale is excellent for a whole winter.

choices.text: Order the koi restocked and say nothing

effects.log: The pond is full again by spring. The court decides your silence was very deep and wise.

choices.text: Write in the court diary: "A crane came, ate fish, and left"

effects.log: The historians are scandalised. Five hundred years later, a scholar calls it the most honest line in the whole dynasty's records.
