events.text: The memorials say the capital is prosperous and content. You have read ten thousand memorials and they all say this. Tonight you put on a cotton robe and a straw hat, take two guards dressed as porters, and slip out through the kitchen gate into the night market.
events.arc: The Emperor in a Cotton Robe

choices.text: Eat at a noodle stall and listen

effects.log: The noodle seller complains about the night watch, who take a bowl free from every stall. The noodles are very good.

choices.text: Follow a magistrate's runner on his rounds

effects.log: The runner collects a copper from every stall for a "lantern tax" that does not exist. He collects a great many coppers.

choices.text: Visit a teahouse where storytellers mock the court

effects.log: The storyteller does an impression of you that is cruel, accurate and very funny. You tip him generously.

events.text: Near midnight, a fight breaks out in an alley: three men of the night watch are beating a fruit seller who refused to pay. Your guards look at you. The street is watching too, and nobody here knows who you are.
events.arc: The Emperor in a Cotton Robe

choices.text: Step in and stop it yourself, as a stranger

effects.log: "Who do you think you are?" says the watch captain. It is a fair question, and you do not answer it.

choices.text: Have your guards step in, quietly

effects.log: The guards are quick and quiet. The watchmen run. The fruit seller presses a pear into your hand.

choices.text: Watch, and remember every face

effects.log: You watch and remember. The fruit seller limps home. You do not sleep that night.

events.text: At the next morning audience, the Prefect of the Capital reports that the city is peaceful, the markets honest and the night watch beloved by the people. The Son of Heaven is wearing very good robes today, and has a pear on the throne's armrest.
events.arc: The Emperor in a Cotton Robe

choices.text: Ask the Prefect about the lantern tax

effects.log: The Prefect turns the colour of old rice. By evening the lantern tax is gone, and so is the Prefect.

choices.text: Ask the Prefect about the night watch's free noodles

effects.log: The Prefect laughs, then sees your face, and stops. The noodle sellers of the capital eat better that year.

choices.text: Summon the watch captain to the throne room

effects.log: The watch captain is brought in, looks up at the throne, and recognises the stranger from the alley. He faints.

choices.text: Say nothing, eat the pear, and change things slowly

effects.log: You change things slowly, over years. The fruit seller never learns why the watch stopped coming.

events.text: Years later you slip out through the kitchen gate once more, in the old cotton robe. The noodle stall is still there, run by the seller's daughter now. She serves you a bowl and says the watch has been honest for years, ever since some strange business in an alley nobody can explain.
events.arc: The Emperor in a Cotton Robe

choices.text: Ask her what the people say about the throne

effects.log: "That it listens," she says, and shrugs. "Sometimes. Eat your noodles."

choices.text: Pay for every bowl at the stall that night (20 taels)

effects.log: The whole street eats free noodles on the emperor's coin, and none of them ever know.

choices.text: Eat in silence and go home before dawn

effects.log: The noodles are as good as ever. You go home through the kitchen gate with broth on your sleeve.

events.text: The Hall of Records is on fire. Clerks form a bucket line from the well; it is hopeless. Inside, on the third floor, are two hundred years of land deeds. You could go up the wall in three breaths with your qi, and every clerk in the line would see it.

choices.text: Go up the wall and throw the deeds out of the window

effects.log: You climb the wall like a cat in a burning house. Deeds rain down into the courtyard. Forty clerks stare up at you, open-mouthed.

choices.text: Go in through the smoke at ground level, like an ordinary fool

effects.log: You come out coughing with an armful of deeds and a singed hat. Ordinary courage. Nobody suspects anything else.

choices.text: Join the bucket line and let the archive burn

effects.log: The archive burns to the ground. Two hundred years of deeds become ash and argument.

events.text: The morning after, the clerks are whispering. A junior clerk named Mo, who saw everything from the bucket line, comes to you with a polite face and says only: "I have always wanted a promotion."

choices.text: Get Mo the promotion

effects.log: Mo becomes Senior Clerk and is grateful in a careful, watchful way. You will be paying for this for years.

choices.text: Tell Mo the smoke plays tricks on the eyes

effects.log: "It does," Mo agrees, "very often." Then Mo bows and leaves, unconvinced.

choices.text: Tell Mo the truth and ask for silence as a friend

effects.log: Mo listens, says nothing for a long time, and then laughs. "I knew the deeds did not fly by themselves."

events.text: A message comes from the palace: the Emperor wishes to thank whoever saved the land deeds of the Hall of Records. A eunuch waits at your door. Behind him, by chance or not, stands a quiet man in grey who belongs to the secret imperial guard.

choices.text: Accept the thanks and say you were lucky

effects.log: The Emperor thanks you for your luck. The man in grey writes something down and leaves without a word.

choices.text: Let Mo receive the thanks instead

effects.log: Mo kneels before the throne and tells a beautiful story about a brave clerk with wet sleeves. Mo is very convincing.

choices.text: Tell the man in grey the truth, before anyone else does

effects.log: The man in grey listens, nods, and says that the throne has uses for people who can climb burning walls. You are not dismissed. Yet.

events.text: The Hall of Records is rebuilt in stone. At the opening, the clerks hang a plaque by the window you once climbed: "Here the deeds flew out". Mo, now senior and plump, gives you a look that could mean anything at all.

choices.text: Take Mo to dinner, and finally talk about it

effects.log: Over noodles, Mo says it plainly: "I would have climbed too, if I could." The secret feels lighter, shared.

choices.text: Avoid the window for the rest of your career

effects.log: You walk the long way round the window every day for years. The clerks think you are superstitious.

choices.text: Pay for the new archive's fire buckets (30 taels)

effects.log: Two hundred new buckets, painted red. Mo signs for them with a perfectly straight face.

events.text: At the Lantern Festival banquet, a servant pouring wine for the Minister of Rites drops the jug and draws a knife. Everyone else is too slow. You are not slow; you have not been slow since your third year in the mountains, and the knife is a breath from the Minister's throat.
events.arc: A Knife at the Lantern Banquet

choices.text: Catch the knife hand with the speed you really have

effects.log: Your hand closes on the assassin's wrist before anyone sees you move. The whole banquet sees the result.

choices.text: Throw your wine cup, as hard as an official plausibly could

effects.log: The cup hits the assassin on the ear. It is a very good throw for a scholar. The guards do the rest.

choices.text: Shout for the guards and do nothing else

effects.log: The guards arrive late. The Minister is wounded, not killed, and you feel the shame of it for a year.

events.text: The assassin is a cultivator of a small demonic sect, hired by a merchant the Minister of Rites had ruined. In the cells, the assassin asks to see you, by name, and says to the guards: "I want to meet the scholar who moves like a mountain disciple."
events.arc: A Knife at the Lantern Banquet

choices.text: Go and see the assassin

effects.log: The prisoner looks at you through the bars and smiles. "I knew it," says the assassin. "You hide well, but you breathe like us."

choices.text: Refuse the meeting, and ask for a fast trial

effects.log: The trial is fast. The assassin is sentenced to labour on the Great Wall, still smiling.

choices.text: Send the assassin a book of the classics

effects.log: The book is returned with one line written inside the cover: "You still breathe like a mountain disciple."

events.text: The Minister of Rites, recovered, invites you to his house to thank you. Over tea he says, quite mildly, that he has been thinking about how you moved, and that he knows what the murim-court pact says about officials who hide their cultivation.
events.arc: A Knife at the Lantern Banquet

choices.text: Tell him the truth and trust him

effects.log: The Minister nods. "A life saved buys a secret kept," he says. "Once." He pours more tea.

choices.text: Talk your way around it: you trained with a sword master as a child

ok.log: The Minister accepts the story, or pretends to. Either way he never mentions it again.

fail.log: The Minister smiles politely and writes a quiet letter to the palace that evening.

choices.text: Ask him what the assassin told the guards

effects.log: "Only that you breathe like a mountain disciple," the Minister says. "The guards thought it was poetry."

events.text: Someone is shouting your name outside your gate at midnight, and it is not the name you use at court. It is {npc}, who trained beside you on the mountain for six years, very drunk and very happy, demanding to spar "like the old days" in front of half the street.

choices.text: Drag {npc} inside before the neighbours wake

effects.log: You haul {npc} through the gate by the collar. {He} is singing the sect's training song, every verse.

choices.text: Pretend not to know {him}, and have the watch take {him} away

effects.log: The watch drags {npc} off, still shouting your mountain name. Several shutters open on the street.

choices.text: Go out and spar, fast and quiet, just to shut {him} up

effects.log: Three moves, and {npc} is sitting in the dust laughing. The street sees two drunks wrestling. Probably.

events.text: The next morning {npc}, sober and ashamed, explains: the sect fell on hard times, {he} is going north to join a caravan guard, and wanted to see you once before going. Your steward, meanwhile, has been asking the neighbours what that strange name meant.

choices.text: Give {npc} money for the road (40 taels)

effects.log: {npc} refuses twice and accepts the third time, with a bow from the old days.

choices.text: Tell the steward it was an old nickname from school

effects.log: The steward accepts it. The neighbours prefer a better story, and invent one.

choices.text: Find {npc} in the watch cells and apologise

effects.log: {npc} looks at you through the bars and says nothing at all. You pay the fine and walk out together, in silence.

events.text: A letter from the north, years later: {npc} is a caravan captain now, with a scar, a family and a camel called Second Elder. The letter is addressed to your court name, carefully, and signed with a drawing of the mountain.

choices.text: Write back, using the mountain name

effects.log: You write the old name for the first time in years. It looks strange in your own hand, and very good.

choices.text: Burn it, to be safe

effects.log: The letter burns. You keep the drawing of the mountain, folded small, inside your official seal box.

choices.text: Send a gift for the camel

effects.log: The camel receives a silk halter fit for a minister's horse. {npc} writes that it has become unbearable.

events.text: A fever is going round the palace, and the Emperor orders every official examined by the Imperial Physician, old Doctor Hua, who can read a pulse like a ledger. Your turn is tomorrow. A cultivator's pulse is slow, deep and strong as a river; no scholar's pulse has ever sounded like that.

choices.text: Spend the night suppressing your qi into the lowest meridians

effects.log: By dawn your pulse is thin and nervous, like a clerk's. Your whole body aches as if you had been folded in a box.

choices.text: Report sick, and miss the examination

effects.log: You stay home with a fake cold. The palace notes your absence, and Doctor Hua writes your name on a separate list.

choices.text: Go as you are, and trust the doctor's discretion

effects.log: You walk into Hua's room with your river of a pulse and offer your wrist.

events.text: Doctor Hua takes your wrist, closes his eyes, and is silent for far too long. Then he takes the other wrist. Then he looks up at you over his spectacles. Outside, the next official in line coughs nervously.

choices.text: Hold still and keep your qi down

effects.log: Hua frowns, nods, and writes "weak spleen, too much reading". You leave, aching and safe.

choices.text: Meet his eyes and say nothing

effects.log: "Interesting," Hua murmurs. "Very good health. Remarkably good." He writes something you cannot read.

choices.text: Ask whether something is wrong

effects.log: "Nothing at all," Hua says, too quickly. "Eat more pears."

events.text: Weeks later Doctor Hua's apprentice arrives at your door with a basket of pears and a sealed note. It reads: "A pulse like a mountain river. I have written 'weak spleen'. Physicians keep many secrets. Please do not make me keep two."

choices.text: Send Hua a gift of rare mountain herbs, in thanks

effects.log: Hua sends back a recipe for a tonic that, he says, would suit a person with an unusually deep river.

choices.text: Burn the note and eat the pears

effects.log: The pears are sweet. The note is ash. You resolve never again to have a fever in this palace.

choices.text: Visit Hua and ask him to treat the poor clerks for free, at your cost (40 taels)

effects.log: Hua agrees. The clerks of the records office are healthier than they have been in years, and never know who paid.

events.text: At the dedication of the new Temple of Heavenly Peace, the great bronze bell is being hoisted into its tower when a rope snaps. The bell, heavier than an ox cart, swings loose above a crowd of officials, monks and children. You are standing directly beneath it.

choices.text: Catch it

effects.log: You catch the bell. Forty officials, two hundred monks and one very small child watch you hold up a ton of bronze with both hands.

choices.text: Throw the child clear and dive aside like anyone would

effects.log: The bell crashes into the flagstones and cracks. The child is unhurt. Nobody looks twice at you.

choices.text: Push the bell's swing aside with a palm strike nobody can see

effects.log: A ripple of qi, a twitch of your sleeve, and the bell falls a yard to the left, onto an empty cart. A miracle, says the abbot.

events.text: The abbot declares that a miracle saved the temple. Some officials have their own explanation, and it is not divine. A monk who stood beside you says nothing, but bows to you a little deeper than to anyone else.

choices.text: Go along with the miracle

effects.log: The abbot has a stone carved: "Heaven held the bell". You attend the carving ceremony with a straight face.

choices.text: Tell the officials you were lucky with the angle

effects.log: Nobody believes you. Several officials begin, very politely, to stand further away from you at audiences.

choices.text: Ask the monk what he saw

effects.log: "I saw a sleeve move," the monk says. "I have seen sleeves move like that before, at Shaolin." He smiles.

events.text: A summons comes from the palace, not about the bell, about something else entirely, or so the letter says. In the anteroom there is a quiet man in grey whom you have never seen before. He looks at your hands for a long time before he speaks.

choices.text: Tell him the truth: you hid what you were, and you would do it again

effects.log: The man in grey nods. "Most of them lie," he says. "You will be hearing from us." Then he lets you go.

choices.text: Talk about the weather

effects.log: He talks about the weather too, for a long time. Neither of you mentions the bell. It is a very frightening conversation.

choices.text: Insist it was a miracle

ok.log: The man in grey sighs and lets the miracle stand. "Heaven held the bell," he repeats, without belief.

fail.log: "Heaven," he says, "does not have calluses on its palms." He makes a note in a small black book.

events.text: The bell is recast and rehung. On the day it first rings again, the abbot invites you to strike it. A crowd gathers. The monk who saw your sleeve move stands nearest, holding the beam out to you with both hands.

choices.text: Strike it gently, as a scholar would

effects.log: The bell sounds soft and long over the city. Nobody sees anything unusual. The monk smiles anyway.

choices.text: Strike it with a breath of qi behind the beam

effects.log: The bell rings so deep that pigeons rise from every roof in the capital. People speak of it for years.

choices.text: Hand the beam to a child from the crowd

effects.log: The child strikes it with all their strength. The note is thin and joyful, and the crowd cheers.

events.text: Every month the garrison holds a wrestling ring, and every month your men ask you to step in. Your officers say it is good for morale. You say your back is bad. Your back is not bad; your back could lift a millstone, and if you wrestle, someone will notice.

choices.text: Step into the ring and lose on purpose

effects.log: You lose to a skinny archer in a way that took more skill than winning. The men cheer the archer.

choices.text: Step in and win, carefully, like a strong farmer

effects.log: You win three bouts like an ox, slow and heavy. Nobody sees a cultivator. They see a very strong officer.

choices.text: Keep refusing, and judge the bouts instead

effects.log: You judge fairly. The men start calling you "the old back" behind your shoulders.

events.text: A veteran sergeant named Bao, who fought cultivators on the southern border twenty years ago, watches you after the ring. Later he comes to your tent and asks if he can see your hands. "Farmers," Bao says, "have calluses here. You have them there."

choices.text: Show him, and ask him to keep it quiet

effects.log: Bao looks at your palms, nods, and says "I fought beside one like you, once". He never says another word about it.

choices.text: Tell him you used to work a forge

effects.log: "A forge," Bao agrees, and spits. "A forge on a mountain, with a sect banner over it."

choices.text: Order him back to his post

effects.log: Bao salutes and goes. That night you hear him telling the story of the southern border, very loudly, to the whole camp.

events.text: Raiders hit the supply wagons at dawn, and the skinny archer from the wrestling ring is pinned under an overturned cart with three raiders closing in. You are the only one near enough to reach the archer in time, and you would have to move faster than any soldier can.

choices.text: Move

effects.log: You cover thirty paces in a breath, lift the cart, and throw the raiders into the ditch. The whole company sees it.

choices.text: Shout for Bao and fight like a soldier

effects.log: Bao arrives at a run with two men. Together you reach the archer, slowly, with a broken arm between you.

choices.text: Throw your spear from where you stand

ok.log: The spear flies far, fast and true. The raiders scatter. The archer limps back to camp, and calls it a lucky throw.

fail.log: The spear falls short. The archer is taken prisoner, and you will spend a year getting the archer back.

events.text: A censor named {npc} has been assigned to review the records of every official who entered service in your year. {npc} is patient, thorough and polite, and {he} has just discovered that you spent six years of your youth at a mountain monastery that has no record of any monks.
events.arc: The Censor with a Long Memory

choices.text: Explain that it was a private academy, long since closed

effects.log: {npc} writes it down. "How sad," {he} says. "So many good academies close."

choices.text: Invite {npc} to inspect the monastery yourself

effects.log: {npc} raises an eyebrow and accepts. The mountain is three weeks away, and {he} seems to look forward to it.

choices.text: Ask an old friend in the Ministry of Personnel to lose the file (50 taels)

effects.log: The file goes missing. {npc} notices that it has gone missing, and opens a new file about that.

events.text: {npc} starts arriving early to audiences to watch you climb the palace steps. {He} has noticed that you never breathe hard, never sweat in summer, and once caught a falling teacup without looking. The file, {npc} mentions, is getting rather thick.
events.arc: The Censor with a Long Memory

choices.text: Start climbing the steps slowly, panting a little

effects.log: You pant convincingly up a hundred steps every morning. {npc} watches, and makes a small note: "theatrical".

choices.text: Confront {npc}: what does {he} want?

effects.log: "The truth," {npc} says. "I am a censor. It is the only thing I collect."

choices.text: Take {npc} to the mountain, as promised

effects.log: Three weeks of mule tracks. At the top, the old abbot of the mountain pours {npc} tea and talks about honour for an hour.

events.text: {npc}'s report is due at the Censorate. The whole of your court career will rest on what {he} writes, and you both know it. On the last evening, {npc} comes to your study, sits down without being asked, and lays the file on your desk.
events.arc: The Censor with a Long Memory

choices.text: Ask {npc} what {he} saw on the mountain

effects.log: {npc} closes the file. "I saw an honest abbot and a good school," {he} says. "The report will say a private academy."

choices.text: Tell {npc} everything, and let {him} decide

effects.log: {npc} listens to the whole story without a word, then takes the file and leaves. You hear nothing for a month. Then a man in grey visits.

choices.text: Argue that the pact itself is unjust

ok.log: {npc} hears you out and, to your surprise, agrees. The report is a masterpiece of saying nothing.

fail.log: {npc} says the law is the law, and takes the file to the Censorate that night.

choices.text: Ask whether the lost file was ever found

effects.log: "It was," {npc} says, very mildly. "In your friend's stove." The report is long, and unkind.

events.text: Years later {npc} becomes Chief Censor, still patient, still polite. At a banquet {he} raises a cup to you across the hall, and then, very slowly and deliberately, lets a teacup slip from {his} other hand, watching to see if you catch it.
events.arc: The Censor with a Long Memory

choices.text: Let it fall and smash

effects.log: The cup smashes. {npc} laughs aloud, for the first time anyone at court can remember.

choices.text: Catch it, without looking

effects.log: You catch it. {npc} bows very slightly. Nothing is ever said, and nothing ever needs to be.

choices.text: Raise your own cup in return

effects.log: You toast each other across the shattered porcelain. The court wonders what on earth that was about.

events.text: A team of four imperial horses bolts in the Avenue of Heavenly Streets, dragging a loaded tribute wagon straight toward a school procession of small children with paper lanterns. The crowd scatters. You could stop the horses with one hand on the bridle, and nobody who saw it would ever forget it.

choices.text: Seize the lead horse and stop the team dead

effects.log: Four horses and a wagon stop as if they had hit a wall. The children stare. So does a eunuch on a balcony.

choices.text: Wave your sleeves and shout, to turn the horses aside

effects.log: The horses swerve into a fruit stall instead. The children are safe, the oranges are not.

choices.text: Cut the traces with a hidden flick of qi

effects.log: A sound like a whip, unseen. The traces part, the horses run free, and the wagon rolls to a stop in the gutter.

events.text: The teacher of the procession finds you that evening and thanks you, bowing so low that her hat falls off. Then she asks, very quietly, whether you would come to the school and teach the children to be brave. A eunuch's servant has also been asking questions in the avenue.

choices.text: Visit the school and tell the children a story about horses

effects.log: Forty children listen to a story about a stubborn horse who learned manners. Nobody asks how you stopped the real one.

choices.text: Find the eunuch's servant first, and ask what he wants

effects.log: The servant wants nothing, he says, except a strong person to carry tribute boxes for the Inner Court. Very strong. For pay.

choices.text: Keep your head down for a month

effects.log: You keep your head down. The story of the avenue grows a little stranger in every teahouse, without you.

events.text: The Inner Court does not forget a useful secret. The eunuch from the balcony, Chief Steward Rong, sends a card: he would hate for anyone to report a hidden cultivator to the Censorate, and he would love for someone to escort a tribute wagon, privately, to a house in the hills.

choices.text: Refuse, and let him do his worst

effects.log: Rong does nothing at all for a year. Then he dies of an ordinary cold, and his secrets die with him.

choices.text: Escort the wagon, once, and look inside

effects.log: The wagon is full of stolen tribute silk. You deliver it, and send its whole inventory to the Censorate, unsigned.

choices.text: Agree, and become Rong's quiet errand-runner

effects.log: You carry Rong's boxes into the hills for two years. You are never exposed. You are never quite free either.

events.text: Your handler in the secret imperial guard is {npc}, who looks like a retired bookseller and once, they say, held a pass alone against a demonic sect. Tonight {npc} hands you a cup of tea and a name: a Vice Minister who meets a masked cultivator every month at a pawnshop by the West Gate.

choices.text: Watch the pawnshop from the rooftops

effects.log: Three nights on cold tiles. On the fourth, the Vice Minister arrives in a hired sedan and leaves with a lacquer box.

choices.text: Pose as a customer and pawn something

effects.log: You pawn a jade comb. The pawnbroker looks at your hands for one breath too long before writing the ticket.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why the guard does not simply arrest the Vice Minister

effects.log: "Because then we would never meet the one in the mask," {npc} says, and refills your cup.

events.text: The masked cultivator comes at last, from a demonic sect, carrying army maps in a lacquer box: maps the Vice Minister has been selling page by page. On the way out the masked one stops in the street below you and says, without looking up: "Come down, rooftop. Your breathing is too loud."

choices.text: Come down and fight the masked one in the alley

ok.log: A short, silent fight among the rain barrels. The masked one escapes over the wall, but leaves the lacquer box behind.

fail.log: The masked one is faster. You wake in the gutter with a headache, and the box is gone.

choices.text: Follow instead, at a distance

effects.log: The trail leads you all night through the city, then vanishes into the river mist by the salt docks.

choices.text: Stay still and let the masked one go

effects.log: A soft laugh from the street, and the masked one walks away. You have the voice now, and the walk, and that is something.

events.text: {npc} hears your report in silence, then burns it in the brazier, page by page. "The Vice Minister will be arrested tomorrow for gambling debts," {he} says. "Nobody will ever know about the maps. Nobody will ever know about you. That is the work."

choices.text: Ask {npc} how {he} bears it, a life nobody will ever know

effects.log: {npc} smiles for the first time. "I keep a garden," {he} says. "The cabbages know."

choices.text: Ask for the masked cultivator's case

effects.log: {npc} hands you a thin file. "Ten years," {he} says. "The masked one was never caught. You are welcome to try."

choices.text: Ask about the pawnbroker who looked at your hands

effects.log: The pawnbroker, {npc} says, has been the guard's eyes at the West Gate for thirty years. You were being tested.

events.text: Envoys from the steppe arrive tomorrow to sign a peace, and the secret guard has word that someone at court wants the peace to fail. You are assigned to the palace kitchens for one night, dressed as a cook's assistant, with a needle of silver for testing dishes and orders to trust no one.

choices.text: Test every dish, one by one, through the night

effects.log: Two hundred dishes, one silver needle. By dawn your eyes ache and your needle is still bright.

choices.text: Watch the cooks instead of the food

effects.log: The head cook, Old Lady Tan, never stops moving. A young pastry cook keeps looking at the door.

choices.text: Make friends with Old Lady Tan, who knows everything

effects.log: Tan feeds you dumplings until midnight and tells you which cooks owe money to whom.

events.text: At the third hour a eunuch you have never seen comes in with an order from the Inner Court: the honey cakes for the envoys are to be sweetened with a special honey, from a small jar he carries. Your silver needle, touched to the jar, stays bright. Something still feels wrong.

choices.text: Follow the young pastry cook, who has slipped out

effects.log: The pastry cook goes to the well and is about to drop a packet in. You catch the wrist. The packet is not sugar.

choices.text: Ask Tan whether she knows this eunuch

effects.log: Tan looks at him once. "Never seen him," she says, "and I know every eunuch who has ever stolen a dumpling."

choices.text: Take the jar and taste the honey yourself

effects.log: It is honey. Good honey. You have tested nothing, and now your mouth is sweet and your doubts are worse.

events.text: Dawn. The envoys are at the gate, the cakes are on their trays, and you have one hour before the banquet begins. Whatever happened in the kitchen tonight, nobody but the guard will ever know.

choices.text: Report the plot to the guard and let the banquet go on

effects.log: The banquet goes ahead. The steppe envoys sign the peace, eat the cakes, and ask for the recipe.

choices.text: Have every dish replaced, all of it, at once

effects.log: The kitchen cooks a second banquet in an hour. Old Lady Tan swears at you for a week, and then sends you a dumpling.

choices.text: Eat one of each dish yourself before they go out

effects.log: You eat a whole banquet in an hour. Nothing happens except that you cannot move until noon.

events.text: The steppe peace holds for years. One autumn a parcel reaches you from the kitchens, by way of the guard: a honey cake and a scrap of paper in Old Lady Tan's rough hand. "Retired," it says. "Still know every eunuch. Still owe you a dumpling."

choices.text: Visit Tan in her retirement

effects.log: Tan lives above a dumpling shop and feeds you until you cannot stand, and tells you three things the guard should know.

choices.text: Eat the cake, and test it with silver first

effects.log: The needle stays bright. The cake is perfect. You laugh at yourself alone in the dark.

choices.text: Send Tan a pension from your own salary (40 taels)

effects.log: Tan sends it back with a note: "Insulting." Then a second note: "Fine. Thank you."

events.text: Dismissed in scandal, struck from the rolls, too famous to hide and too disgraced to employ. In the teahouses the storytellers have already made you a legend: the official who hid a mountain's worth of cultivation under a scholar's robe. The real you is sitting in the corner, paying for its own tea.

choices.text: Buy the teahouse, which is for sale (200 taels)

effects.log: You own a teahouse now. Customers come to see the legend pour tea. The tea is mediocre and the queues are long.

choices.text: Correct the storyteller's mistakes, loudly, from the corner

effects.log: The storyteller is furious, then delighted. From now on the story includes a heckler in the corner, who is also you.

choices.text: Leave the capital for a quiet village

effects.log: You go south to a village with one well and no storytellers. Within a year, someone tells your story there too.

events.text: Old colleagues start to appear, never by daylight. A clerk with a question about grain law. A magistrate with a dispute he cannot solve. A frightened young official who has just been offered a bribe and wants to know what you would do.

choices.text: Give advice freely, and ask nothing

effects.log: Your corner of the teahouse becomes a court of its own. Half the capital's honest officials pass through it in a year.

choices.text: Charge a fair fee for counsel

effects.log: Ten taels a question. The advice is good and the business is brisk, and slightly shameful.

choices.text: Send them all away: the court is no longer your concern

effects.log: They stop coming. The teahouse is very quiet, and you find you miss the questions.

events.text: A eunuch from the palace arrives at the teahouse in a plain sedan with a sealed message. The Emperor has heard that the disgraced official's teahouse gives the best advice in the capital, and would like a copy of the tea list, and of the advice.

choices.text: Send the tea list and a long memorial on everything you have heard

effects.log: The memorial is read. Two ministers are quietly dismissed, and your teahouse receives a plaque in the imperial hand: "Clear Water".

choices.text: Send the tea list only

effects.log: The palace receives the list, tastes the tea, and sends a polite note saying it is mediocre. It is.

choices.text: Send nothing: the court dismissed you, let it stay dismissed

effects.log: No answer. But from then on, a plain sedan stops outside every month, and someone inside listens.

events.text: Years have passed since the scandal. A young official in fine robes comes into your teahouse corner with a familiar look: the face of someone hiding a mountain's worth of cultivation under a scholar's robe. You know the breathing.

choices.text: Warn the young official, quietly, of everything that happened to you

effects.log: The young official listens, pale, and leaves without finishing the tea. You hope it was enough.

choices.text: Say nothing, and pour more tea

effects.log: The young official drinks and goes. Some lessons nobody can teach.

choices.text: Tell the story aloud, to the whole teahouse, as a storyteller would

effects.log: The teahouse roars at your version of your own scandal. The young official laughs loudest, and understands.

events.text: At your dismissal hearing, the decisive testimony came from {npc}, who had shared an office with you for nine years. Now {npc} stands at your gate in the snow, demoted, ill and alone, because the faction that bought the testimony has since thrown {him} away too.

choices.text: Let {npc} in, and give {him} the warm room

effects.log: {npc} sits by the brazier and cannot look at you. You pour tea. Nobody speaks for an hour.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why, before {he} comes one step closer

effects.log: "They had my brother's debts," {npc} says. "I chose the family. I would choose it again."

choices.text: Close the gate

effects.log: The gate closes. Snow falls on {npc}'s shoulders. In the morning there are only footprints, going away.

events.text: {npc} recovers slowly in your house. One evening {he} brings out a ledger, copied in secret during the years of the scandal: the names of every official the faction bribed, and how much, and when. Your own name is not in it. Yours, {npc} says, was the case they paid the most to ruin.

choices.text: Take the ledger, and plan what to do with it

effects.log: The ledger goes under a floorboard. For the first time in years you feel something other than tired.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the ledger should be burned; the past is past

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. "You are a better person than me," {he} says, and does not burn it.

choices.text: Ask whether the brother's debts were paid

effects.log: "Paid," says {npc}, "and gambled again in a month." You both laugh, which surprises you both.

events.text: Spring. The faction that ruined you both is in power at court, and a new Chief Censor has been appointed who is said to be honest and to hate that faction. {npc}, well again, is packing to leave the capital for good.

choices.text: Take the ledger to the new Chief Censor together

ok.log: The Chief Censor reads it in a single night. Eleven officials fall. Your name is cleared in the court gazette, and so is {npc}'s.

fail.log: The Chief Censor is less honest than advertised. The ledger vanishes, and {npc} leaves the capital that same night.

choices.text: Walk {npc} to the city gate and say goodbye as friends

effects.log: At the gate {npc} bows to the ground. "Nine years in one office," {he} says. "I should have been worth more of them."

choices.text: Give {npc} money for a new life in the south (60 taels)

effects.log: {npc} goes south to teach in a village school. Every New Year a crate of oranges arrives, without a note.

events.text: Your patron, the Marquis of Linyang, pays well and asks little. Today he asks one thing: in the next volume of your novel, could the villainous general who burns the river city be changed into a heroic general who saves it? The general in question, by an unlucky coincidence, was the Marquis's great-grandfather.

choices.text: Rewrite the chapter as asked

effects.log: The general saves the city. Readers find the chapter oddly flat. The Marquis weeps with pride.

choices.text: Refuse: the river city remembers what happened

effects.log: The Marquis is silent for a long time. Then he stops paying, very politely.

choices.text: Make the general complicated: guilty, and sorry

effects.log: You write a general who burns the city and spends the rest of his life rebuilding it. It is the best chapter you have written.

events.text: The new volume reaches the river city, where old men still point to the scorched stones by the bridge. A delegation of booksellers from there arrives at your door with a question that is also a warning.

choices.text: Tell them the Marquis paid for the change

effects.log: The river city booksellers print a pamphlet. Your novel is now famous in a way you did not intend.

choices.text: Show them the chapter about guilt and rebuilding

effects.log: The booksellers read it standing in your doorway. One old man asks if he may read it aloud at the bridge.

choices.text: Promise them the truth in the next volume

effects.log: They go home satisfied, and every bookseller in the province waits for the next volume.

events.text: The Marquis of Linyang sends for you. The old man has read every version, including the one you did not publish, and sits holding a box of his great-grandfather's letters, unopened for a hundred years.

choices.text: Open the letters with him

effects.log: The letters are full of apology and lists of rebuilt houses. The Marquis reads them aloud, and you write them into the next volume, word for word.

choices.text: Return to his patronage, on your terms

effects.log: The Marquis agrees to everything. "Write him as he was," he says. "I would rather be ashamed of the truth than proud of a lie."

choices.text: Thank him and find a new patron

effects.log: You leave the Marquis with his letters. A bookseller in the river city offers you patronage, paid in fish.

events.text: Your new novel features a eunuch who controls an emperor through a pet parrot. The Board of Rites has declared it "disrespectful to the Inner Court" and ordered every copy burned. Booksellers are already selling the burned copies, which are surprisingly intact, at three times the price.

choices.text: Write a public apology to the Inner Court, in the parrot's voice

effects.log: The apology is so funny that it is banned too. Sales triple again.

choices.text: Withdraw the novel and lie low

effects.log: The novel vanishes from the shelves and reappears under them. You stay home for a month.

choices.text: Write the sequel, in which the parrot is burned

effects.log: The sequel is darker and much better. The Board of Rites does not know what to do with it.

events.text: A eunuch of the Inner Court arrives at your door, alone, holding a copy of the banned book with every page carefully annotated. He wants to know, very seriously, how you knew about the parrot.

choices.text: Tell him the parrot was invented

effects.log: "Invented," the eunuch repeats, with deep suspicion. "The parrot's name was Jade Tongue. Did you invent that too?"

choices.text: Offer him tea, and ask about his notes

effects.log: His notes are excellent. He has corrected eleven details of palace life and suggested a better ending.

choices.text: Ask him to leave

effects.log: He leaves the annotated copy on your step. It is the best review the book ever gets.

events.text: The scandal grows: there was a real parrot, and a real eunuch who trained it, and an old minister has stood up at court to ask how a novelist knew. Your next book will be read, or burned, by everyone.

choices.text: Write a memoir explaining it was all coincidence

effects.log: The memoir is read as a confession. The real eunuch is quietly retired, with his parrot, to a monastery.

choices.text: Publish the sequel, in which the parrot speaks the truth

effects.log: The sequel sells out in a day. The Board of Rites bans it, and then, quietly, reads it in committee.

choices.text: Write about something else entirely, a love story among fishermen

effects.log: The fishermen's love story is gentle, unbannable and beloved. Nobody mentions parrots again.

choices.text: Buy a parrot and teach it to recite the classics (30 taels)

effects.log: The parrot learns two lines of the Analects and one word that would get you banned again.

events.text: Some years on, the Board of Rites holds an exhibition of banned books, so that officials may know what to ban. Yours has a place of honour, in a glass case, with a stuffed parrot beside it borrowed from a monastery.

choices.text: Visit the exhibition, disguised

effects.log: You stand at your own glass case, eavesdropping. A young clerk tells his friend the book changed his life.

choices.text: Write to ask for the parrot to be returned to its owner

effects.log: The parrot goes home to the old eunuch's monastery, where it recites the Analects to the monks.

choices.text: Ask for royalties on the exhibition

effects.log: The Board of Rites replies with forty pages explaining why not. You frame them.

events.text: Three days after the list goes up, the most famous matchmaker in the capital arrives at your door with a red card and a painted fan. Grand Secretary Wen, the most powerful minister at court, would like the Top Scholar to marry into the Wen family. The card bears the name {npc}, and an excellent horoscope.

choices.text: Agree to meet {npc} before anything is decided

effects.log: The matchmaker looks at you as though you had asked to taste a melon before buying it. Then the meeting is arranged.

choices.text: Agree at once: the Grand Secretary is the Grand Secretary

effects.log: The matchmaker is delighted. Wine is opened. The Grand Secretary sends a jade horse.

choices.text: Refuse: you will not be bought along with your hat

effects.log: The matchmaker snaps the painted fan shut. By evening the whole capital knows, and the Grand Secretary's house is very cold.

events.text: You meet {npc} in the Wen family's pear garden, chaperoned by four aunts and a parrot. {npc} has read your palace essay, disagrees with the third section, and says so within a quarter of an hour, while the aunts pretend to be deaf.

choices.text: Argue the third section, properly

effects.log: You argue until the parrot falls asleep. {npc} wins on two points. You have never enjoyed losing so much.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what {he} wants from a marriage

effects.log: "A house with a library," {npc} says, "and nobody telling me to stop reading." One aunt coughs.

choices.text: Talk only of pleasant things, as is proper

effects.log: You talk of the weather and the pear blossom. {npc} is polite, and very bored, and so are you.

events.text: Negotiations begin. Grand Secretary Wen wants the wedding before the spring audiences, and wants you in the Wen faction by summer. The Pure Stream scholars send a note warning that Wen's son-in-law will never be trusted by honest men again.

choices.text: Tell Wen you will marry {npc}, not the faction

effects.log: Wen laughs, not unkindly. "Everyone says that," says the Grand Secretary. "Let us see."

choices.text: Ask {npc} privately what to do

effects.log: {npc} reads the Pure Stream note and tears it in half. "My father's faction is my father's," {npc} says. "Not mine."

choices.text: Withdraw politely, citing the horoscope

effects.log: The horoscope is reconsulted and found, conveniently, to be unlucky. {npc} sends back your poems without a note.

events.text: The wedding day is set, the red sedan is ordered, and the Wen household is in uproar. On the last evening {npc} sends a message by a maid: a single line, "Do you still want the library?"

choices.text: Send back: "Only if we share it." Marry {npc}

effects.log: You are married under the pear trees with half the court watching. The library is shared, and argued in, for the rest of your lives.

choices.text: Marry {npc}, and refuse the Grand Secretary's faction on the wedding day

effects.log: At the feast you toast the Grand Secretary and decline the Wen faction in the same breath. {npc} laughs aloud. The marriage begins well.

choices.text: Break it off, with regret

effects.log: You send back the red card. {npc} keeps the essay with the third section underlined, and marries a provincial governor two years later.

events.text: A Count's house of the north proposes a match between your family and theirs, with {npc} as the intended. The match is good; the problem is the dowry. They want to send forty chests of goods, and they want your house to send forty back, and your house has, if you are honest, about eleven chests' worth.

choices.text: Accept, and borrow to fill the chests (150 taels)

effects.log: The chests are filled with borrowed silk and one very old bronze tripod. Your accountant stops sleeping.

choices.text: Write to the Count's house, honestly, about the eleven chests

effects.log: Your letter is either insulting or refreshing. Nobody in either house can decide which.

choices.text: Ask to meet {npc} first

effects.log: You meet in a teahouse, chaperoned by two stewards counting chests in their heads. {npc} rolls both eyes at them.

events.text: A letter arrives from {npc}, not from the Count's house: "I have seen the forty chests my family is sending. Most are full of things nobody has used in sixty years, including a ceremonial helmet for a horse. Please do not ruin yourself to match them."

choices.text: Write back and suggest twenty chests each, of useful things

effects.log: {npc} replies within a day: "Seeds, books, a good loom, and absolutely no helmet." The families are scandalised and secretly relieved.

choices.text: Write back thanking {npc}, and fill the chests anyway

effects.log: Your pride sends forty chests. {npc} is touched, and slightly worried about your finances.

choices.text: Return the borrowed silk and send the eleven chests you have

effects.log: Eleven chests go north. The Count's house is silent for a month.

events.text: The Count's house sends its answer: a proposal from {npc}'s grandmother, who rules the house, that the two families stop counting chests and start counting grandchildren. The old matriarch would like to see the match made before the plum blossoms fall.

choices.text: Marry {npc}, with twenty chests of seeds and books

effects.log: You are married in the plum season. The seeds are planted, the books read, and the horse's helmet is never seen again.

choices.text: Marry {npc}, with whatever chests you have

effects.log: The wedding is modest and merry. The grandmother dances, which nobody has seen in twenty years.

choices.text: Decline: the houses want different things

effects.log: The proposal ends with courteous letters. {npc} sends one more, privately, about the horse's helmet, and it makes you laugh for a week.

events.text: The Chief Eunuch's adopted family, rich, powerful and loathed by every honest minister, proposes a marriage between you and their ward, {npc}. It would make you the Inner Court's in-law. It would also make you, overnight, untouchable at court.
events.arc: The Proposal from the Inner Court

choices.text: Meet {npc}, without promising anything

effects.log: {npc} arrives with a book of Pure Stream poetry, which in that house is a kind of rebellion.

choices.text: Refuse outright

effects.log: The refusal is read aloud in the Chief Eunuch's hall. Your next three memorials are lost in the palace post.

choices.text: Accept: power is power

effects.log: The Inner Court sends a jade belt and a list of favours they will expect. The list is long.

events.text: {npc} asks to speak with you alone, by the palace moat. "They chose you because you are honest," {npc} says. "An honest in-law is worth ten bought ones. I do not want to be the price of you."
events.arc: The Proposal from the Inner Court

choices.text: Ask {npc} what {he} wants instead

effects.log: "To leave that house," {npc} says, "and teach girls to read in some county where nobody knows the name."

choices.text: Say that you could marry {him} and still refuse the Inner Court

effects.log: {npc} laughs, almost kindly. "Nobody refuses them from inside," {he} says. "I have watched for twenty years."

choices.text: Thank {npc} and end it there

effects.log: You part by the moat. {npc} walks back toward the palace without looking round.

events.text: The Inner Court wants an answer before the New Year. Whatever you choose, {npc} will pay for it in that house. A eunuch waits at your gate each morning for the answer, polite and patient as a heron.
events.arc: The Proposal from the Inner Court

choices.text: Refuse the match, and find {npc} a teaching post in a far county

effects.log: You refuse. A month later {npc} leaves the capital in a plain cart with a crate of books. A letter comes each spring, full of pupils.

choices.text: Marry {npc}, and leave the court together

effects.log: You resign your post, marry {npc}, and go south together. The Inner Court never forgives either of you, and never finds you.

choices.text: Refuse the match, as gently as such things can be done

effects.log: The refusal is polite. {npc} sends a single line: "Thank you for not buying me."

events.text: Two noble houses have feuded over the river meadows for three generations, and yours is one of them. The Duke of the province, tired of both, proposes an end to it: a marriage between your house and the other, with {npc} of the rival house as the match. Both families are horrified.

choices.text: Agree to the Duke's proposal

effects.log: The elders of your house stop speaking to you. The rival house's elders stop speaking to {npc}. It is, at least, a start.

choices.text: Ask to meet {npc} on the disputed meadow itself

effects.log: You meet in the middle of the river meadow, by the boundary stone. {npc} has brought a picnic, and a map with all three generations of claims.

choices.text: Refuse: the feud is your family's honour

effects.log: The Duke sighs and finds another solution: the ducal house takes half the meadow.

events.text: {npc}'s grandfather and your oldest great-aunt have each written to the Duke that they will not attend any wedding. Meanwhile, servants from both houses have started meeting at the meadow, curious, bringing tea.

choices.text: Invite both elders to the meadow, together

effects.log: The two old people sit on opposite sides of the boundary stone for an hour in silence. Then they argue about whose grandfather cheated at chess.

choices.text: Visit {npc}'s grandfather alone, with a gift

effects.log: The old one receives you coldly and keeps you three hours. At the end, the gift is accepted, and so, perhaps, are you.

choices.text: Let the servants' tea do the work

effects.log: By midsummer the servants of both houses are intermarrying. The elders have lost control of the situation entirely.

events.text: The Duke sets a date. Both houses send their banners to the meadow, and for the first time in three generations they fly side by side over the boundary stone. The servants of both houses have already set out the tea.

choices.text: Marry {npc} at the boundary stone

effects.log: You marry on the meadow, with both banners flying. Your great-aunt cries, and claims it is the pollen.

choices.text: Marry {npc}, and give the meadow to the villagers as common land

effects.log: The feud ends with nobody owning the meadow at all. The villagers graze their goats there and toast you both every spring.

choices.text: Call it off: the peace can stand without a marriage

effects.log: The banners come down, but the feud does not return. {npc} sends a pot of tea every spring, from the meadow.

events.text: At a poetry gathering in the provincial capital, the best poem of the evening is by {npc}, the child of a poor village teacher, who wrote it on the back of a tea bill. Your noble relatives, who arranged the gathering to find you a match among the Counts' families, do not notice {npc} at all.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to read the poem aloud again

effects.log: {npc} reads it again. The Counts' families stop talking. Your aunt, who arranged the evening, starts to look very worried.

choices.text: Buy the tea bill with the poem on it (20 taels)

effects.log: {npc} sells it, laughing, and pays the teahouse with the money. You keep the poem in your sleeve for a month.

choices.text: Meet the Counts' families as your relatives intend

effects.log: You meet six young nobles of excellent family and forget all of their names by morning.

events.text: You and {npc} meet again, and then again, at the village teacher's house, which has a leaking roof and more books than chairs. Your relatives find out. Your aunt arrives with a list of reasons, beginning with "rank" and ending with "the roof".

choices.text: Have the teacher's roof mended, before anything else (40 taels)

effects.log: The roof is mended. {npc}'s father, the teacher, receives you the next week with the best tea in the house.

choices.text: Tell your aunt that rank is a title, not a person

effects.log: Your aunt says that is the sort of thing poets say. You say {npc} is a poet. The conversation ends badly.

choices.text: Ask {npc} whether {he} even wants a noble's life

effects.log: "I want a life with poems in it," {npc} says. "I do not know yet whether yours has room."

events.text: Your house's elders meet in council. They can refuse to bless a match beneath your rank; they can also, quietly, be persuaded. {npc} waits in the village, writing a poem about waiting, which is very good.

choices.text: Marry {npc}, with or without the council's blessing

effects.log: You marry in the village teacher's house, under the mended roof. The council sends a gift late, and then, slowly, its blessing.

choices.text: Bring the teacher to speak before the council

effects.log: The old teacher speaks to the elders of your house for an hour about the classics. The council is defeated by quotation. You marry {npc} that autumn.

choices.text: Let it go, for the good of your house

effects.log: You do not marry {npc}. Years later you read a famous poem about a noble who chose a title over a tea bill, and know whose it is.

events.text: {npc}, your eldest, is old enough to be named Crown Heir, and the ministers want the old tests applied: a judgement on a real case, an essay before the court, and a season governing a province. The Board of Rites has prepared the first case already: two villages and one well.

choices.text: Let {npc} judge the well case without your help

effects.log: {npc} spends three days at the well, listens to both villages, and orders a second well dug. The ministers are impressed, the villagers delighted.

choices.text: Advise {npc} privately before the judgement

effects.log: Your advice is good. {npc}'s judgement is good. The ministers notice that it sounds very like you.

choices.text: Skip the tests: {npc} is the heir because you say so

effects.log: The ministers bow. The Board of Rites writes the tests down as "waived", in very small characters.

events.text: The essay before the court is on the duties of a ruler. {npc} stands before three hundred officials and reads it in a clear voice, and you realise halfway through that it contains a criticism of your own salt tax.

choices.text: Smile, and let the court see you smile

effects.log: The court relaxes. The Son of Heaven can be criticised by the heir, and smiles. Several ministers write that night to {npc}.

choices.text: Interrupt and ask {npc} to explain the salt passage

effects.log: {npc} explains it, calmly and well, with figures. The court holds its breath. You have no answer.

choices.text: Let it pass in silence, and speak to {npc} afterwards

effects.log: Afterwards {npc} kneels and says: "You taught me to say what is true. I did not know you meant to the throne too."

events.text: Last, the province. {npc} is sent to govern the hill province of Yunzhong for a season, the poorest in the empire. Reports come back: rice prices down, a bandit chief pardoned and made a road builder, and one very angry local governor.

choices.text: Name {npc} Crown Heir before the whole court

effects.log: {npc} kneels before the throne in yellow robes. The court shouts ten thousand years. It sounds, for once, as if they mean it.

choices.text: Ask the angry governor to court to hear the other side

effects.log: The governor complains for an hour. Every complaint turns out to be a reason the people of Yunzhong love {npc}.

choices.text: Wait another year: the throne is not a prize for a good season

effects.log: {npc} accepts the wait with a bow. The court watches the heir, the ministers write letters, and the year is long.

choices.text: Name {npc} heir, and ask for the salt tax essay as {npc}'s first edict

effects.log: {npc}'s first act as Crown Heir lowers the salt tax. The villages hear of it, and the new heir is loved before being crowned.

events.text: A cousin from the elder branch of your house has petitioned the Board of Rites: the title, the petition claims, should pass to the elder branch, not to your eldest, {npc}. The claim rests on a will from your great-grandfather's time that nobody has seen in sixty years, and that the cousin has suddenly found.

choices.text: Have the will examined by the Board's experts

effects.log: The experts squint at the will for a week. The paper is old. The ink, they say, is curious.

choices.text: Let {npc} answer the petition

effects.log: {npc} writes a reply that is polite, careful and devastating. You did not know your child could write like that.

choices.text: Offer the cousin money to withdraw (100 taels)

effects.log: The cousin takes the money, withdraws, and files a new petition a month later with better lawyers.

events.text: The Board of Rites holds a hearing. The cousin brings witnesses: two old servants who swear the will is real, and a calligrapher. {npc} sits beside you and watches the witnesses with great attention.

choices.text: Ask the Board to test the will's ink against the year it claims

effects.log: The ink is made with a pine soot first sold in the capital eleven years ago. The cousin's calligrapher leaves very suddenly.

choices.text: Let {npc} question the old servants

effects.log: {npc} asks them gently about the great-grandfather's dogs, horses and favourite dishes. Neither servant has ever met the old one.

choices.text: Argue the house's history before the Board yourself

ok.log: You speak for an hour about the house and its debts and its people. The Board finds for your line.

fail.log: The Board is unmoved, and postpones the decision for a year.

events.text: The claim collapses. The cousin is disgraced, and the elder branch of the family has nowhere to live: their house was mortgaged to pay the lawyers. {npc} comes to you and asks what is to be done with them.

choices.text: Let {npc} decide

effects.log: {npc} gives the cousin's family a farm on the estate and the cousin a job: keeping the house records. "Where I can see the ink," {npc} says.

choices.text: Give the elder branch a house and a pension (80 taels)

effects.log: The elder branch moves into a small house by the river. The cousin is ashamed for a year, then useful for twenty.

choices.text: Leave them to their own mortgage

effects.log: The elder branch scatters. {npc} says nothing, and you see in that silence what kind of head of the house {npc} will be.

events.text: Years later the cousin, now the house's record keeper, brings you a dusty box found in the attic: the real will of your great-grandfather, sixty years lost. It leaves everything to your line, and adds a note: "Look after the elder branch. They were always bad with money."

choices.text: Show it to {npc} and laugh together

effects.log: {npc} reads it and laughs until the tea spills. "The old one knew," says {npc}. "Sixty years ago, the old one knew."

choices.text: Give the will to the cousin to keep

effects.log: The cousin holds it a long time, then puts it in the record room under lock and key, without a word.

choices.text: Have it read aloud at the New Year feast

effects.log: The whole house hears the great-grandfather's joke. Even the elder branch laughs, eventually.

events.text: A winter fever lays you low for a month. When you can sit up again, the Chancellor reports that the court has been asking a question nobody dared to ask aloud before: if the throne were ever empty, who would hold it for {npc}, your eldest? The Chancellor, it seems, would be willing.

choices.text: Name {npc} to sit in the audiences beside you, from now on

effects.log: {npc} takes the small chair beside the throne. The Chancellor's smile becomes fixed, and stays fixed.

choices.text: Ask the Empress Dowager's view

effects.log: The old woman says one sentence: "Never give a regency to a Chancellor." Then the Dowager asks for more tea.

choices.text: Thank the Chancellor for such loyalty

effects.log: The Chancellor bows very low. You notice, when the Chancellor rises, a set of new rings.

events.text: {npc} has watched the audiences for a season and has views. One evening {npc} comes to your sickroom with a list: the ministers who visited the Chancellor during your fever, and how long each one stayed.

choices.text: Read the list with {npc}, name by name

effects.log: Eleven names. Some surprise you. One makes you put down your tea. {npc} says nothing, and waits.

choices.text: Tell {npc} that spying on ministers is beneath an heir

effects.log: "So is being deposed," says {npc}. You laugh until you cough, and then you read the list.

choices.text: Burn the list: a ruler must trust somebody

effects.log: The list burns. {npc} watches it go with a face you cannot read.

events.text: You are well again, but older, and the question will come back. The court waits for an edict on the regency, if the worst should happen. The Chancellor has begun arriving early to every audience, wearing all the new rings.

choices.text: Name a council of three, the Chancellor not among them

effects.log: The edict names three honest ministers. The Chancellor is posted, with great honour, to rebuild the southern canals.

choices.text: Name {npc} of age, with no regent at all

effects.log: The edict declares the heir fit to rule alone. The court is astonished. {npc} kneels and does not speak for a long time.

choices.text: Name the Empress Dowager as regent, as the Dowager advised

effects.log: The old woman accepts with a sniff. Nobody at court will try anything while the Dowager lives, and the Dowager plans to live a long time.

choices.text: Leave the question open, as rulers always have

effects.log: No edict. The Chancellor keeps the rings. {npc} keeps the list, in a new copy.

events.text: By custom, the title passes to {npc}, your eldest. But your house's steward, who has served thirty years, comes to you with a ledger: under {npc}'s management of the eastern farms, the harvests have fallen two years in a row, while a younger child's farms have doubled.

choices.text: Ask {npc} about the eastern farms

effects.log: {npc} explains: the tenants were starving, so the rents were cut. The harvests fell; the tenants lived. "I would do it again," {npc} says.

choices.text: Inspect the farms yourself, unannounced

effects.log: The tenants on the eastern farms are thin but alive. The younger child's tenants are richer and very quiet.

choices.text: Tell the steward that custom is custom

effects.log: The steward bows and closes the ledger. The steward's opinion is perfectly clear.

events.text: Word gets round the house that you are weighing the succession. The younger child's supporters among the servants grow bolder; {npc} grows quieter. At dinner nobody speaks of anything but the weather, for a month.

choices.text: Give {npc} the hardest task the house has: settle the mill dispute

effects.log: {npc} settles it in a week, with patience, a pot of tea and a joke about millstones that both families retell for years.

choices.text: Speak to the younger child about the quiet tenants

effects.log: The younger child admits it: the rents were raised and the tenants were told to say nothing. The doubled harvests were bought.

choices.text: End the talk: announce that nothing will change for now

effects.log: The house calms. Everyone still watches everyone else across the dinner table.

events.text: The Board of Rites expects your house to register an heir before the New Year. The steward stands by with the brush and the register. {npc} is in the next room, waiting to hear. The whole house has found reasons to be in the corridor.

choices.text: Register {npc}, by custom and by merit

effects.log: {npc} is registered as heir. The steward, who has seen the mill and the tenants, signs as witness without a word.

choices.text: Register {npc}, and make the tenants' rent cut the law of the house

effects.log: {npc} becomes heir, and the rent cut becomes permanent. The eastern farms hold a festival that lasts three days.

choices.text: Register the younger child, for the harvests

effects.log: The younger child is registered. {npc} bows, says nothing, and leaves to take up a post far from the house.

choices.text: Register {npc}, simply because {npc} is the eldest

effects.log: Custom wins. {npc} becomes heir without a test, and spends years proving it was right anyway.

events.text: A farmer runs into the hall of {ct_fief} without taking off his straw hat. On the eastern horizon the sky has gone brown and is humming. Locusts, a cloud of them two days wide, and the millet is one week from harvest.
events.arc: The Day the Sky Ate the Millet

choices.text: Call every village out with gongs, drums and nets

effects.log: For three days {ct_fief} beats every pot it owns. The cloud thins, swerves, and eats only the eastern half.

choices.text: Burn the stubble of the east fields as a firebreak

effects.log: The smoke turns the cloud south, onto the neighbour's land. Your farmers cheer; the neighbour sends a very long letter.

choices.text: Offer incense at the temple of the Harvest God

effects.log: The incense is thick and the prayers loud. The locusts, who are not religious, eat almost everything.

events.text: The harvest comes in at half its weight. The granary of {ct_fief} could feed everyone thinly until spring, or it could be sold in the city, where grain prices have doubled since the cloud passed over three counties.
events.arc: The Day the Sky Ate the Millet

choices.text: Open the granary and ration it fairly

effects.log: Every family gets its measure, stamped by your seal. Nobody grows fat; nobody starves.

choices.text: Sell half in the city while the price is high

effects.log: The carts come back heavy with silver. The farmers watch them pass and say nothing at all.

choices.text: Lend the grain against next year's harvest

effects.log: The loans are fair and recorded. The farmers are fed, and in debt to you, and both of you know it.

events.text: In spring old Granny Tao from the duck pond asks to see you. She says the locusts laid their eggs in the eastern dirt, and ducks eat locust eggs like dumplings. She has thirty ducks. She would like three hundred.
events.arc: The Day the Sky Ate the Millet

choices.text: Buy the ducks, all three hundred (60 taels)

effects.log: A white river of ducks marches across the east fields. No locust hatches that year, and {ct_fief} eats very well at New Year.

choices.text: Have the villages plough the eggs under instead

effects.log: The ploughing works, mostly. Granny Tao says the ducks would have done it better, and cheaper.

choices.text: Ask the gong-beaters to march with the ducks

effects.log: The same villagers who beat the locusts away now herd ducks to drums. It becomes a festival, and then a tradition.

events.text: It has rained for nineteen days. The river below {ct_fief} is the colour of tea and rising a hand's width every hour, and the old dyke at Willow Bend has begun to weep through its stones. Below the dyke sit three villages.

choices.text: Lead the villagers on the dyke all night with sandbags

ok.log: By dawn the dyke holds, with you asleep on it in the mud. The villages wake up dry.

fail.log: The dyke breaks an hour before dawn. Everyone gets out, but the three villages are under water to the eaves.

choices.text: Cut the dyke upstream and flood the empty reed marsh

effects.log: The river pours into the marsh, drowning the best duck hunting in the province. The villages stay dry.

choices.text: Evacuate the villages and let the river do as it likes

effects.log: Everyone climbs to the temple hill with their pigs. The river takes the houses and leaves the people.

events.text: When the water goes down it leaves mud, a drowned ox on a roof, and a hundred families sleeping in the temple. The provincial office has promised relief. The provincial office promises many things. Somebody has already named the ox.

choices.text: Pay to rebuild the houses at once (150 taels)

effects.log: New houses go up before the autumn winds. The families paint your name above their doors, a little crookedly.

choices.text: Write to the province and wait for the relief silver

effects.log: You write politely. Then less politely. The families spend a long season on the temple floor.

choices.text: Give the families timber and let them build for themselves

effects.log: They build fast, and badly, and proudly. One roof faces the wrong way and its owner refuses to discuss it.

events.text: The relief silver arrives at last, carried by Eunuch Fang of the provincial office, who counts it out in front of you and keeps a third of it on his side of the table. "Handling," Fang says, and sips your tea.

choices.text: Smile, sign for the full sum, and remember the eunuch's name

effects.log: Fang leaves pleased. You write his name in a small book you keep for such names.

choices.text: Refuse to sign until every tael is on your side

ok.log: Fang laughs, then sees your face, and pushes the third across. "A misunderstanding," the eunuch says.

fail.log: Fang takes all of it back to the province. "Next year, perhaps," the eunuch says.

choices.text: Report the eunuch to the Censorate

effects.log: The Censorate thanks you for your diligence. Nothing else happens, for a long time.

events.text: The new dyke at Willow Bend is finished in stone, not earth. The villagers ask what should be carved on the capstone. The masons suggest the date. The headman suggests your name. A small girl suggests a fish.

choices.text: Carve the names of those who carried sandbags

effects.log: Every name goes on the stone, in small neat characters. People walk out on holidays to touch their own.

choices.text: Carve a fish, as the girl asked

effects.log: A large, cheerful fish now watches the river. Children say it keeps the water polite.

choices.text: Carve the eunuch's name, under the word "Handling"

effects.log: Fang's name sits on your dyke forever, above a very pointed word. The province pretends not to see it.

events.text: The salt carts that cross the Ox Horn Hills into {ct_fief} have started paying a toll to someone who is not you. The carters call the toll-taker Iron Pot, after the helmet. Iron Pot is polite, takes exactly one sack in ten, and gives receipts signed {npc}.
events.arc: The Toll on the Salt Road

choices.text: Send the militia into the hills

effects.log: The militia spend a week in the hills and find only cold campfires and a receipt, addressed to you.

choices.text: Ride a salt cart yourself, dressed as a carter

effects.log: You sit on the salt for two days. On the third, a figure in an iron pot steps onto the road and asks for one sack in ten.

choices.text: Ignore it: one sack in ten is cheaper than a war

effects.log: The toll goes on. The salt merchants raise their prices by one sack in ten.

events.text: The toll-taker's name is {npc}. Under the iron pot is a tired face and a soldier's posture. {npc} deserted from the frontier after a flood year, came home to find no home, and led thirty starving neighbours into the hills.
events.arc: The Toll on the Salt Road

choices.text: Offer the band work as wardens of the salt road

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. "Wages?" Wages. "Receipts?" Receipts. The band comes down from the hills.

choices.text: Hand {npc} to the magistrate

effects.log: {npc} goes to the prefecture in chains, without a word. The thirty neighbours scatter into the hills again.

choices.text: Let {npc} go, on a promise to leave the road

effects.log: {npc} keeps the promise. The salt comes through untaxed, and the hills are quiet, and empty.

events.text: Three years on, the Ox Horn Hills are the safest road in the province. Then a real gang from the next county tries the salt road, forty riders with no receipts. Your wardens are outnumbered and holding the pass.
events.arc: The Toll on the Salt Road

choices.text: Ride to the pass with every militiaman you have

effects.log: You arrive as {npc} is holding the narrow bend with an iron pot and a long spear. Together you drive the riders off.

choices.text: Send word to the prefecture for soldiers

effects.log: The soldiers come a week late. The road is clear by then; somebody cleared it, and nobody asks who.

choices.text: Pay the new gang to go elsewhere (80 taels)

effects.log: The gang takes the silver and goes to rob the next county instead. It is not a proud solution.

events.text: Your steward {npc} keeps the books of {ct_fief} in a hand like printed type. Every harvest comes in at a round number: three thousand measures, never three thousand and eleven. Fields, you have noticed, are not so tidy.

choices.text: Read the old ledgers yourself, at night

effects.log: By the third lamp you find it: the round numbers began the year {npc} took the keys.

choices.text: Ask the village headmen what they actually paid

effects.log: The headmen give odd, honest numbers: three thousand and two hundred, three thousand and ninety.

choices.text: Praise {npc} for such tidy work

effects.log: {npc} bows very low. The next ledger is even tidier.

events.text: Following the difference, you find a second granary, behind a mill in the next valley, registered to a cousin of {npc}. It is half full. The other half has been sold, a cart at a time, for six years. The cousin, the miller says, has never once been seen.

choices.text: Confront {npc} with both ledgers in the hall

effects.log: {npc} reads them, and puts them down, and does not deny a single number.

choices.text: Set a trap: let it be known the tax inspector is coming

effects.log: That night the second granary's carts move. Your men are waiting on the road.

choices.text: Dismiss {npc} quietly, with no inquiry

effects.log: {npc} leaves the next morning with one small trunk. Nobody in {ct_fief} knows why, and everybody guesses.

events.text: {npc} asks to speak alone. Half the stolen grain, {npc} says, went to the hill village of the lepers, which the old master of {ct_fief} ordered unfed. The rest bought a cousin's freedom from a debt. "I kept good books," {npc} says. "Just two of them."

choices.text: Check the story in the hill village yourself

ok.log: The village elders know {npc} by name and bow at it. The story is true, at least half of it.

fail.log: The village is empty: the people moved west last winter. You will never know.

choices.text: Keep {npc} as steward, with one ledger and an open grant to the hill village

effects.log: {npc} keeps the books for twenty more years, in odd, honest numbers. The hill village is fed by name.

choices.text: Send {npc} to the magistrate: theft is theft

effects.log: The magistrate sentences {npc} to three years of labour. The hill village sends one basket of persimmons, unsigned.

events.text: The autumn fair is the one week a year when {ct_fief} feels like a city. The merchants' guild sends a delegation to ask about stall fees. They would like them lower. Your treasury would like them higher. Everyone would like an opera.

choices.text: Halve the stall fees

effects.log: Twice as many stalls open. The fair stretches to the river and you cannot find your own horse.

choices.text: Double the fees: the fair needs you more than you need it

effects.log: The fees come in; half the merchants go to a rival fair two counties away.

choices.text: Hire an opera troupe from the capital (70 taels)

effects.log: The troupe plays The White Snake for three nights. The fair is packed, and the guild forgets its complaint.

events.text: On the last day two farmers drag one goat to your seat of judgment. Farmer Su says he bought it at noon. Farmer Ren says he bought it at noon too. The goat's former owner has left the fair with two purses. The goat is eating your sleeve.

choices.text: Untie the goat and see which farmer it walks to

ok.log: The goat walks straight to Farmer Ren, who is holding a turnip. Justice is served, and so is the turnip.

fail.log: The goat walks to you and will not leave. Both farmers are paid out of your purse, and the goat lives in your stable.

choices.text: Make both farmers co-owners, in alternate months

effects.log: Su and Ren share the goat for eleven years. They become inseparable friends, mostly through arguing.

choices.text: Send the constables after the man with two purses

effects.log: The constables catch him at the ferry. Both farmers get their money back, and the goat goes to auction.

events.text: The fair has grown every year since. The guild now wants a charter: its own hall, its own scales, and its own judge for small disputes. It would mean more trade, and one less thing you control in your own fief.

choices.text: Grant the charter

effects.log: The guild hall goes up by the river with your seal over the door. Trade doubles; the guild's judge is very fond of goats.

choices.text: Refuse it: the scales stay in your hall

effects.log: The guild grumbles, then stays. The fair keeps growing, a little slower and a little sulkily.

choices.text: Grant it, on condition the troupe returns every year

effects.log: The guild agrees with a groan. The opera comes back every autumn, and {ct_fief} is famous for it.

events.text: The bronze bell of Clear Spring Temple cracked in the frost and now sounds like a dropped pot. The abbot, an elderly monk named Huiming, comes to {ct_fief}'s hall with a bowl, a smile, and a figure written on a slip of paper.
events.arc: The Cracked Bell of Clear Spring

choices.text: Pay for a new bell (120 taels)
